en: The *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Devaputra Susīma*, Scroll One.

Entitled "The Dharma Words Proclaimed by Mañjuśrī," also known as "The Dharma for Severing Doubt Regarding All Dharmas," and also known as "The Universal Entry into the Expedient Wisdom and Discerning Illumination of the Buddhas' Dharmas.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
1. Chapter One: Inquiry on the Four Matters. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery, together with a great assembly.

There were one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, ten thousand bodhisattvas, as well as devaputras of the desire realm, devaputras of the form realm, and devaputras of the universal purity realm, along with bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One was surrounded by and seated in an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of beings as he preached the Dharma.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī and the Devaputra Susīma were seated within the assembly.

When the Devaputra Susīma observed that the assembly was settled, he rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; may the Buddha graciously analyze and explain its resolution?"
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent,
O Devaputra!”
"Seeking the supreme meaning for all in the world, you have asked the Tathāgata with this very thought.
Speak what you doubt; ask whatever you wish!
Suṣṭhitamati, the Devaputra, leaping up in joy, immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining non-deceptive faith and being intent upon the Mahāyāna?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being firm and resolute in their actions, and not becoming timid or weak?”
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining unsurpassed and most excellent merit?
What is meant by a bodhisattva knowing the practice that is free from all obstructions?
What is meant by a bodhisattva departing from the dust of darkness and attaining wisdom?
What is meant by a bodhisattva entering an assembly with courageous eloquence and attaining fearlessness?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the meaning of what has been heard and relying upon it for protection?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the profundity of the Dharma and transcending the mundane?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining reverent and compliant practice of the Buddha, the World-Honored One’s teachings?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the reception of the Dharma-teachings and guiding and benefiting all beings?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the wisdom of unsurpassed supernormal powers?
What is meant by a bodhisattva who, when demons manifest strange apparitions, remains unmoved in mind?
What is meant by a bodhisattva who attains profound and far-reaching wisdom that cannot be overtaken?
What is meant by a bodhisattva who is not defiled by worldly dharmas?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining entry into profound practice that is supreme and without peer?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining knowledge of skillful means and faculties, and preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitude?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining entry into the gates of liberation, such that while remaining within birth and death, they do not encounter form or desire?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining extraordinary skillful means, such that they subdue arrogance?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the skillful means of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-upāya*) and knowing all that is done?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the skillful means of discipline (*vinaya-upāya*) and being free from all views?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the skillful means of excellent expedient means (*kuśala-vidhi-upāya*) and nurturing all beings?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining auspicious vows, with body and mind purified?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the power of patience, with a mind free from anger?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the pāramitās, crossing over to the other shore?
What is meant by a bodhisattva obtaining what is needed to remedy deficiencies and benefiting all beings?
What is meant by a bodhisattva becoming beloved and respected by all people in the world?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining wisdom and discernment, such that they are praised by others?
What is meant by the inexhaustible merits practiced by a bodhisattva?
What is meant by a bodhisattva strengthening their fundamental resolve so as to inevitably attain Buddhahood?
What is meant by a bodhisattva always being noble and honored, grasping all dharmas and attaining mastery?
"What is meant by a bodhisattva who, in whatever they undertake to give or create, always acts as a teacher?
What is meant by a bodhisattva who maintains all matters through dhāraṇī, such that there is nothing they do not understand?
Having asked this, the Devaputra Susīma remained silent.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent,
Son of Heaven Susīma!"

Your question is profound; you have brought much benefit to the people of the world. By recollecting and upholding this matter, you have questioned the Tathāgata, giving rise to the bodhicitta to deliver and liberate others from birth and death.
"Listen attentively and receive this with care!
The Buddha shall explain its meaning for you, surpassing what you have asked, so that you may swiftly attain this matter.
Thereupon, the devaputra received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"A bodhisattva has four practices by which they attain non-deceptive faith and resolve upon the Mahāyāna.
What are these four?"
First, by means of skillful expedients, they enter into wisdom without wavering;
second, by establishing great compassion, they abide in unobstructed loving-kindness;
third, by establishing the principles of the Dharma, they are able to respond to whatever is questioned.
Fourth, by establishing oneself in the Way and attaining supernormal powers, one thoroughly understands all that exists.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains non-false faith and resolves upon the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Steadfast in skillful means, Having realized wisdom that is bottomless,
Universally practicing great compassion, He protects beings with kindness so they may always attain liberation."
Having attained the skillful means of the Dharma that accords with reality, one’s responses are free from obstruction;
through supernatural powers one masters the Path and transforms others, and having attained this, none can destroy it.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva’s actions become firm and steadfast,
and he does not fall into cowardice. What are these four?
First, diligence that does not waver;
second, purity of one's own physical conduct as well as purifying others;
third, a mind that is pure and virtuous, thereby attaining the Way.
Fourth, they achieve accomplishment without weariness toward the Buddha-dharma.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva’s actions become firm and steadfast, such that they do not fall into cowardice or weakness.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Attaining firm abiding in diligence, Established in the Middle Way, free from the two extremes,
Ever pure and without defilement— So it is with the actions of body, mind, and speech."
One's actions are always pure and virtuous;
for this reason, one follows the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching, never wearying of seeking instruction, and constantly contemplates the Buddha-dharma.
These four matters are supreme among all dharmas; they constitute the subtle and wondrous upholding.
If there are those who firmly abide in these dharmas, they shall immediately attain the path of practice.
Having already mastered both the internal and external, they will fully reach the stages of the Way.
"Abiding within these three states, he shall become a Dharma King before long.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven,
there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains unsurpassed and most excellent merit."
What are these four matters?
First, to extensively instruct all bodhisattvas through the perfection of wisdom;
second, to exhort all those who have not yet resolved their minds toward enlightenment to generate that aspiration for the Way.
Third, one should constantly practice the threefold vow:
first, precepts; second, wisdom; third, equanimity. One who accords with these matters should perform meritorious deeds without anger.
Fourth, one should keep the Way in mind without indolence.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains unsurpassed and most excellent merit.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"By means of the perfection of wisdom, One instructs those who are intelligent and wise."
Thus abiding equally in the Way, they constantly use this mind of the Way to widely exhort and encourage all people,
causing them all to resolve upon the aspiration for enlightenment.
Not turning back from the three categories, if there is one who responds accordingly,
they shall accord with the meaning of the Way.
All that they do will result in the fulfillment of merit, gradually drawing them closer to the Way.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva attains knowledge of conduct that is free from all obstructions.
What are these four?
First, in all that one does, one always employs wisdom, never acting with stubbornness or self-will;
second, knowing that all phenomena belong to causes and conditions, one remains free from the notion of "self" and is without anger;
third, one gathers and protects all beings through the dharma of emptiness.
"Fourth, to remain far removed from craving and desire, and to clearly understand the six sense-faculties.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains conduct that is free from all obstructions.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Always act with wisdom; do not be stubborn nor follow your own whims.
Trust in the skillful means of the Vinaya and do not cling to what you see.
This Dharma is characterized by emptiness; never abandon sentient beings."
Having transcended all desires, both internally and externally purified;
through this supreme Dharma established by the four bases of power,
one attains unimpeded wisdom and reaches the perfection of insight.
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
There are four practices by which a bodhisattva leaves behind the dust of darkness and attains wisdom.
What are these four?
First, never being weary or satisfied with what one has heard;
second, preaching the Dharma according to the desires of others without harboring any expectations in one's heart;
third, regarding all that is done as like an illusion, such that wisdom is not impaired within the various realms of phenomena.
The fourth is to simultaneously resolve upon the path and transcend into the city of Dharma.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva leaves behind the dust of darkness and attains wisdom.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Always seeking profound learning, never weary of hearing the Dharma; Thoroughly examining the meaning of the teachings, one responds to those who seek instruction."
Having already attained dhāraṇī, one speaks from one's own intention and no longer receives instruction from others.
Whatever is done is like a dream, a mirage, or an illusion; viewing all phenomena in this way is the nature of delusion.
That which is practiced and established does not destroy the Dharma; by once generating a pure intention, one immediately abandons suffering.
Such categories of Dharma are most extraordinary; this sutra is preeminent and supreme—one should always remain close to it.
Having departed from the darkness and dust of the world, one attains the clarity of wisdom and wanders through the three periods of time, like the light of the sun.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
A bodhisattva has four practices by which they enter into courageous eloquence and attain fearlessness.
What are these four?
First, attaining dharani so that one maintains mindfulness and does not forget.
Second, his speech is able to answer all questions and sever all their doubts;
third, through great compassion he instructs all beings, causing them to enter into emptiness;
fourth, his actions are free from the works of Māra, whereby he attains the wisdom of supernormal powers.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva enters among the assembly with courageous eloquence and attains fearlessness.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Having attained dhāraṇī, One does not forget what has been heard."
His speech answers all inquiries with firmness, severing every doubt;
with great compassion he provides vast instruction that all things are non-existent.
Having fully mastered supernormal powers, the desires of Māra cannot restrain him.
These four dharmas are what makes one a bodhisattva;
thus, being without fear, one dwells among the assembly without dread.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!
A bodhisattva has four modes of practice by which they attain the meaning of what they have heard, relying upon it and maintaining it. What are these four?
First, they retain everything that is heard; yet regarding what is heard and what is not heard, there is neither power, nor grasping, nor any destination.

Second, one distances oneself from all sounds that are not correct practice, understanding that all phenomena are equal in liberation; if one investigates their meaning according to reality, they are like echoes.
Third, if one hears that there is a profound sutra in another region, one disregards one's own body to go and seek it.
Fourth, having entered the meaning of tranquility, one is free from all clamor and distraction.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains the meaning of what has been heard and, relying upon it, maintains protection.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Though one may desire to hear much of the Dharma, If one does not listen to or grasp its meaning..."
Without hearing, there is no power; thus, the meaning is the essential point.
All sounds within the three realms are not the practice of the true path;
they are like echoes, comparable to a scale. Knowing the meaning is likewise so.
Thus having heard and listened, one contemplates and receives its meaning;
do not let the body act on its own—such a teaching brings joy upon hearing.
Its meaning is supreme and foremost; the Dharma is tranquil and free from the meaning of agitation.
"By practicing this profound Dharma, one receives and reveres its meaning.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva may rely upon the depths of the Dharma and transcend the mundane world."
What are the four?
First, gathering a great multitude and preaching the Dharma for them;
second, manifesting the phenomenon of impermanence before the great assembly.
Third, to exhort those who perform great sacrifices to cultivate the vows of awakening;
fourth, to always desire to relinquish all possessions and dwell in secluded places.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains the profound depths of the Dharma and transcends the mundane world.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Abiding in the great city, Always dwelling within it, By means of his wisdom,
he preaches the Dharma."
Abiding at the great assembly of the body, I establish the multitude; amidst lust and negligence, I manifest impermanence for them.
At the great sacrifice, we together assisted; through the encouragement and aid of that sacrifice, I have attained awakening.
"Coexisting with non-existence, always mindful of renunciation, the mind constantly aspires for and seeks dwelling in seclusion.
Furthermore, O Devaputra:
Bodhisattvas have four practices by which they attain reverence and compliance, and carry out the teachings of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
What are these four?
First, their minds are always fixed upon the Path, never departing from it until the ultimate end.
Second, they retain what they have heard and never forget it;
third, they act according to their promises and do not refuse those who come with requests;
fourth, they practice emptiness and enter into all phenomena.
"These are the four matters by which one attains the respect and compliance of Bodhisattvas and carries out the teachings of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Though the body undergoes all manner of painful suffering, The resolve for the Way never turns back."
Having heard the essential points for entering the Dharma, one is then a great guide.
Whatever is promised by mind and speech, the bodily practice likewise accords with those words.
Cultivating the wisdom of all emptiness, one enters the dharmas of the wise and the sagacious.
Practicing according to the Dharma teachings, one attains freedom from lust, anger, and delusion;
without indolence or cessation, one is neither resentful nor remorseful.
One’s name is praised throughout the ten directions, and one’s virtues are sung in hymns of praise.
"If one should accord with this teaching, there will be no fault in their Dharma-wisdom.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva may receive and uphold the teachings of the Dharma, benefiting all beings through the Way."
What are the four?
First, dwelling in the realization of the emptiness of the body, one is able to extensively expound the Great Dharma for the assembly;

second, having already disciplined one's own mind and departed from sensual desire to attain nirvāṇa, one further causes those in the assembly to discipline their minds and cease their desires, preaching the Dharma of nirvāṇa.
Third, having fulfilled the path through one's own practice, one further establishes all beings in the Mahāyāna;
fourth, having personally sought the Dharma and mastered its myriad subtleties, one further teaches others, causing them to seek the Dharma as well.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva receives the teachings of the Dharma and guides and benefits all beings.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"To instruct others, Causing them to receive the essential point of emptiness, To discipline the mind and cease desire,"
Abiding in the state of *nirvāṇa*,
the Virtuous and Most Honored One, endowed with great supernormal powers, bestows the gift of the Dharma and reveals the Vehicle of Awakening to all beings.
Having fully accomplished what was to be done and attained the mind of the Way, he establishes others among the multitude and leads them to the Great Vehicle.
Constantly seeking the Dharma, he accords with the power of its meaning; he preaches the Dharma for the multitude, neither adding to nor subtracting from it.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva attains the wisdom of unsurpassed supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
What are these four?
First, to daily cultivate the four pure practices of brahmacarya;
second, to constantly dwell in secluded and quiet places;
third, to enter deeply into the patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti).
"Fourth, the equality of body, mind, and wisdom.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains the wisdom of unsurpassed supernormal powers.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“Daily cultivating the holy life, one establishes oneself; always delighting in seclusion, one dwells in purity.
Having entered the profound Dharma, one then reaches the Way; with body and mind in equanimity, one personally attains wisdom.”
Having already attained such union with the equality of all practices, they have fully mastered the five supernormal powers.
Flying to the ten directions, they abide before all Buddhas,
providing nurture and support for all people.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva, when Māra manifests strange apparitions, remains unmoved in mind.
What are these four?
First, to cause all who dwell in the four dhyānas to enter into emptiness;
second, to always maintain great compassion and never abandon any sentient being;
third, to provide offerings and support to the Triple Gem with unceasing diligence, never becoming weary or satisfied.
Fourth, by means of *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), the six *pāramitās* are made to abide firmly.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva, when Māra manifests strange apparitions, remains unshaken in mind.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Abiding in emptiness and the absence of conceptual thought, He establishes the four dhyānas of the Path.
With constant and boundless compassion, He causes all beings to peacefully enter into the ultimate meaning."
Regarding the string of the Jewel of the Dharma, it is neither severed nor broken;
corresponding to the various *pāramitās*, this is that which is led by skillful means.
The mind is honored and indestructible, remaining firm and unmoving.
All the four Māras are entirely subdued by him.
Seeing all common folk entangled within the net of Māra,
he reveals the path to Nirvāṇa and causes them all to set forth upon this vehicle.
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva attains profound and far-reaching wisdom that cannot be overtaken.
What are these four?
First, constantly contemplating entry into the profound Dharma;
second, always completely abandoning matters that are not meaningful;
third, constantly feeling concern for all beings, whereby one attains discourse in accordance with the Dharma.
Fourth, they are able to subdue the obstinate and rigid, enlighten the ignorant and deluded, and attain the Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains profound and far-reaching wisdom that cannot be surpassed.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Always contemplate with the mind, Entering into the dharma of emptiness; Relinquish what is not meaningful, And always accord with the right meaning."
Having entered this mindfulness, one brings concern for all beings; attaining profound and far-reaching wisdom, it is the supreme state of mind.
It tames the fierce and stubborn, opens the way for those who are obscured and ignorant, inspires the aspiration for enlightenment, and establishes the Mahāyāna.
The wisdom of supernormal powers has all been accomplished; having attained profound and far-reaching wisdom, it cannot be fathomed.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
A bodhisattva has four practices by which they do not become defiled by worldly dharmas. What are these four?
First, whether one gains profit, or pleasure, or fame, or praise, one does not feel joy.
Second, one does not feel sorrow even when there is no gain, suffering, lack of reputation, or slander.
Third, relying on the experience of the five aggregates, one protects and nurtures all beings.
Fourth, regarding those who have acquired the aggregates, one demonstrates them to be like an empty village.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva does not become defiled by worldly dharmas.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"If there is benefit and renown, One has already attained all happiness."
Even when such praise is bestowed, the mind does not take joy in it;
likewise, when faced with the suffering of lack of profit or fame, the wise do not grieve.
Like a lotus flower unsullied by water, their conduct in the world is just so.
If one employs this principle regarding the aggregate of sensation, thereby protecting and nourishing all beings,
and has already been able to extinguish all aggregates, one regards them as being like an illusion.
Acting in accordance with the Dharma while in the world, they remain unsullied by worldly things;
causing all to attain the meaning of happiness, they take the virtue of their precepts as their unguent.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva enters into profound practice that is supreme and peerless.
What are these four?
First, this body is also devoid of a person;
second, this person is also not a person; third, all dharmas are utterly still and silent;
fourth, wisdom is without attachment.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains entry into profound practice, which is supreme and peerless.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"This body is not a body; This person is not a person."
The stillness of the Dharma is likewise so, and wisdom is also free from desire and attachment.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva attains knowledge of skillful means and the faculties [of beings] to preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude."
What are the four?
First, one immediately attains supernormal powers;
second, one's wisdom is free from all obstructions.
Third, they attain the wisdom of eloquence;
fourth, their original vows are already purified.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva knows the roots of skillful means and preaches the Dharma for the sake of the multitude.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"His supernormal powers have already been perfected, And his wisdom is without obstruction.
His eloquence and insight are always thus; His original vows are completely purified."
Having already known and seen the faculties of others, he preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate;
the listeners immediately hear and accept it, without doubting or being startled by Nirvana.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
A bodhisattva has four practices by which they enter the gates of liberation and, while remaining within the cycle of birth and death, do not associate with form or desire.
What are these four?
First, they dwell in the empty village; if they see those who are bound in captivity, they deliver and liberate them.
Second, they attain the establishment of the signless (*animitta*), whereby all those who practice with attachments are delivered and liberated;
third, they attain the wishless (*apraṇihita*), remaining peaceful, harmonious, concentrated, and secluded, while nurturing all beings;
fourth, they attain skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), manifesting all phenomena through wisdom.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains entry into the gates of liberation and, while remaining within birth and death, does not encounter form or desire.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Having attained emptiness regarding the aggregates, The prisoner is immediately liberated."
Having established oneself in the signless, one transcends all conceptualizations and attachments.
Having attained the wishless, one is serene, harmonious, concentrated, and secluded;
wherever beings are born, one nurtures them all.
When wisdom and skillful means transform and enlighten others, one abides in the gate of liberation;
being fully endowed with these, one enters at the proper time and does not cease within the formless realm.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!
Bodhisattvas have four practices by which they attain extraordinary skillful means and subdue arrogance.
What are these four?
First, they universally observe and fully perceive all dharma-realms.
Second, to understand the root of birth and death and deliver beings from it through the Dharma;
third, to fully know the root of the body’s desires;
fourth, to practice nirvana and have no doubt regarding all dharmas.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains extraordinary skillful means and subdues arrogance.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Universally observing and fully perceiving, All realms of phenomena,"
Ultimately free from any biased or resentful mind, he regards all things with complete equanimity.
Regarding the very foundation of the body, he dwells within desire with sovereign mastery;
having realized its extraordinary excellence, he teaches by responding through skillful means.
There is nothing at all to be practiced; all dharmas are in parinirvāṇa.
Unborn and without destination, all that exists is utterly exhausted.
Without pride or self-conceit, they subdue all arrogance.
"By means of skillful wisdom, they cause all beings to enter nirvana.
Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices of a bodhisattva by which one attains the skillful means of causal conditions and understands all that is done."
What are the four?
First, through giving one attains great wealth; because of this, one achieves this [result].
Second, through upholding the precepts one attains rebirth in heaven; because of this, one achieves this [result].
Third, by studying extensively one achieves great wisdom, and through this, one attains this state;
fourth, through cessation and contemplation one leaves birth and death behind, and through this, one attains this state.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains skillful means regarding causes and conditions and understands all that is done.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Through giving, one obtains great wealth; This is the retribution resulting from those conditions."
Observing the precepts leads to birth in the heavens; this is the fruit and retribution resulting from that cause.
Extensive learning, wisdom, and freedom from desire lead to the heavens; this is the fruit and retribution resulting from that cause.
Practicing the contemplation of the Path and being free from ignorance and attachment lead to the heavens; this is the fruit and retribution resulting from that cause.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva attains skill in the Vinaya and becomes free from all views.
What are these four?
First, while amidst the notion of permanence, the mind attains non-attachment;
second, amidst impermanence, the intention remains unchanged;

third, seeing that all arising things and the root of birth and death are produced from the conjunction of the twelve links of dependent origination, one who has thus seen and known no longer engages in such activities.

Fourth, to observe all arisings and ceasings, as well as the cessation of birth and death, which proceeds from the dispersal and extinction of the twelve links of dependent origination; having already seen and known this, one dwells within the three realms without performing acts of cessation.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains the skillful means of the precepts and becomes free from all views.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"For those who hold the view that things are permanent, He demonstrates the reality of impermanence."
Amidst impermanence, he manifests the Middle Way of the True Dharma.
For the sake of all people, he extensively explains the meaning of causes and conditions;
those who hear these twelve matters attain universal purity of mind.
Throughout all the ten directions, as the World-Honored One has taught:
ignorance is the root of birth and death; from it, the high and the low arise.
All things that thus arise shall likewise never again cease.
The causes and conditions have all been exhausted; he does not participate in the twelve assemblies.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra, there are four practices of a bodhisattva by which one attains skillful means (upāyakauśalya) and nurtures all beings."
What are the four?
First, regarding all people as one's own, manifesting the Way for them all;
second, never becoming weary or satisfied with the meritorious deeds one performs.
Third, dwelling within the cycle of birth and death, they have no seeking for nirvana;
fourth, they enter into liberation according to whatever beings delight in, employing skillful means so as not to be defiled by desire.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains skillful means (upāyakauśalya) and nurtures all beings.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Being firm toward all people, He causes them to abide in the awakening of the Way."
Whatever merits one has performed, one does not think of stopping midway.
While remaining within the cycle of birth and death, one seeks nirvāṇa;
according to what one delights in, one thereby attains liberation.
One should always keep this in mind with the heart and remain close to this Dharma;
through skillful means and expedients, one will come to understand it all thoroughly.
With a constant resolve to nurture and protect, [one benefits] countless multitudes of people.
"Embracing all-knowledge, may they all swiftly attain it.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva attains auspicious vows and achieves purity of body and mind."
What are the four?
First, being free from stinginess and greed;
second, giving without discriminating as to the time.
Third, firmness in the precepts;
fourth, always aspiring toward the Way in all actions of body and mind.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains auspicious vows and purity of body and mind.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“The mind is simple and not stingy; The precepts are pure and without flaw.
Firmly established and unshakable, It is like Mount Sumeru.”
"Whatever is performed by body and mind, one should always aspire to the Vehicle of Awakening;
now that this auspicious response has been attained, such a state will be realized before long.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!"
A bodhisattva has four practices by which they attain the power of patience and their mind remains free from resentment and anger. What are these four?
First, they treat all people as one would one's own parents who love their child, regarding them no differently than oneself.
Second, if one encounters suffering, pain, flogging, or mutilation, one calculates that there is no such thing as a self and thus feels no grief or anxiety;
third, having attained the understanding of emptiness, one is free from all views;
fourth, regarding the evils committed by oneself, one constantly reproaches and repents them, while regarding the deeds of others, one observes them but does not approve.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains the power of patience, such that the mind is free from anger.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Regard all beings as one's own body, Or like parents loving their child."
Constantly maintaining a mind of great compassion, he illuminates and nurtures all people.
If anyone gives rise to a heart of resentment, he perceives it and it is extinguished;
having already understood emptiness, he is able to practice the foremost patience.
If my body has any shortcomings or faults, I shall always deeply reproach and repent for them;
and when I see the flaws and impurities of others, I shall never point out their deficiencies.
All people of every kind, I shall deliver and liberate them all.
Even within the midst of dreams, he never gives rise to a mind of anger.
Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva attains the pāramitās and crosses over to the other shore.
What are the four?
First, the merit one performs is immeasurable;
second, the wisdom one cultivates is limitless.
Third, by means of a single pāramitā, one fulfills all the perfections (pāramitās);
fourth, when generating the aspiration to perform meritorious deeds, one seeks nothing else but the desire for omniscience (sarvajñatā).
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains the pāramitās and crosses over to the other shore.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"In performing meritorious deeds, one never feels satiety, Just as all streams flow back toward the sea."
Cultivating immeasurable wisdom, they have already attained abiding in the Buddha-vehicle.
Thus they uphold the single perfection of the infinite, fulfilling all the *pāramitās*;
whatever they undertake with a resolute mind, they always aspire to seek the True Path.
Having already attained the crossing to the other shore, and likewise with all the *pāramitās*, one then enters the city of Nirvāṇa; thus, it is not difficult to attain.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva obtains what is needed to remedy deficiencies and benefits all beings.
What are these four?
First, they possess inexhaustible treasuries of jewels;
second, they possess infinite teachings of the Dharma;
third, they have already attained mastery of supernormal powers.
"Fourth, his mind is impartial, like the earth.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva obtains what others lack and brings benefit to all.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
That treasury of merit is inexhaustible, and the teaching of the Dharma is likewise endless;
his supernormal powers and wisdom reach everywhere without obstruction, and his mind is as impartial as the earth.
Such a Dharma is difficult to measure; having already attained stability on the Path, one who acts thus brings great benefit and shall swiftly reach Buddhahood.
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
There are four practices by which a bodhisattva becomes honored by all people of the world.
What are these four?
First, practicing the four sublime abodes;
second, practicing the four ways of attracting others to rescue and gather all beings;
third, possessing the wisdom of the four noble truths.
Fourth, they attain the four kinds of non-obstruction:
first, regarding meaning; second, regarding phenomena; third, regarding sequential order; and fourth, regarding response.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva becomes honored by all people in the world.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"As one who dwells as Brahmā practices the four purities, Always delighting in bestowing the four kinds of kindness;
Having already attained the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths, One uses it to make offerings to all people."
Because of this kindness, one has attained deliverance; one should teach and preach the Dharma accordingly.
By acting with kindness, one brings people together; for this reason, one is seen with respect and affection.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva attains wisdom and discernment, and is praised by others.
What are these four?
First, being fully endowed with extensive learning, one does not transgress the precepts and attains freedom from doubt;
second, having attained joyful abiding, one is peaceful and free from harm;
third, having attained tranquility, the sense faculties become concentrated.
Fourth, having already attained peace and security for oneself, one is free from craving; one does not harm oneself in one's actions and fully attains insight and knowledge.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva attains wisdom and sagacity, and is praised by others.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Having heard it, one should fully receive and uphold it; By means of self-restraint, one crosses to the other shore.
One who acts thus has no doubt, And attains the joy of dwelling in a state of peace."
Having already taken up residence in a secluded place, the faculties are then stilled and concentrated;
the body is at peace and free from craving, as one fully perceives all forms of self-inflicted harm.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices of a bodhisattva by which the merit they produce is inexhaustible.
What are these four?
First, having attained abundance through faith;
second, having attained abundance through diligence;
third, having attained abundance through great compassion.
"Fourth, one should dedicate all merit solely to the Mahāyāna.
These are the four matters by which the merit performed by a bodhisattva becomes inexhaustible.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Having attained firm abiding in faith, there is nothing that can shake it;
by constantly practicing the energy of diligence, one thereby gains great power.
With inexhaustible great compassion and boundless pity,"
Constantly for the sake of all people, One practices the broad and great path.
Because of this, one attains inexhaustible merit,
Which gradually increases further until it becomes immeasurable.
"Just as when the moon is full, it is pure and flawless,
ever dwelling among the multitude of stars, its brilliance incapable of being obscured.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!"
A bodhisattva has four practices by which they strengthen their fundamental commitment and will surely attain Buddhahood.
What are these four?
First, that which is spoken with the mouth is not at variance with the body and mind.
Second, having already received and upheld the essentials;
third, the mind being already peaceful and secure, attaining abiding on the Path;
fourth, the will becoming firm and strong, like a diamond.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva strengthens their fundamental resolve and will surely attain Buddhahood.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"What the mouth speaks, What the actions likewise perform, And what one has already revered and loved—"
Upholding the essential teaching, one is already securely established; with this resolute mind toward the Path, one’s body becomes as firm and unyielding as a diamond.
Thus, these constitute the four practices of the Dharma; the wise and discerning person constantly cultivates these matters.
With no hesitation in mind, having attained concentration and firmly established the essentials, they shall surely reach Buddhahood.
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
There are four practices by which a bodhisattva is always upheld by the noble and eminent, grasps all dharmas, and attains mastery.
What are these four?
First, they attain the power of wisdom while lacking the power of desire;
second, they attain the power of discernment and leave behind all darkness of ignorance;
third, their minds attain mastery and do not follow the teachings of Māra.
Fourth, in order to attain dhāraṇī, he preaches the Dharma according to the inclinations of others.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva, as one of noble and honored status, constantly grasps all dharmas and attains mastery.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Having attained courageous wisdom through the power of knowledge, One does not follow the force of craving and desire.
The power of discernment dispels the darkness of delusion, And one has already crossed over and been liberated from all views."
With a mind already honored, all Māras are subdued; having attained dhāraṇī, one responds to questions;
teaching the assembly without self-injury—by these means, one swiftly attains honor.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
there are four practices by which a bodhisattva becomes a teacher for all that is undertaken and performed.
What are these four?
First, being free from anger;
second, always showing respect to others;
third, refraining from sexual misconduct.
"Fourth, their intention is pure and virtuous.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva serves as a teacher for all that they undertake.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"With a mind free from lust and anger, always abiding in reverence,
one attains the pure and virtuous supreme path and becomes a teacher who expounds essential wisdom.
As a master craftsman of various skillful means, he stands above all throughout successive lifetimes."
All people of the world look up to him with reverence, and everyone prostrates themselves before him in worship.
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
There are four practices of a bodhisattva by which he maintains all matters and understands them all without exception."
What are the four?
First, they have mastered wisdom and roam within it, passing through all things without exception;
second, whatever they proclaim, the Buddhas of the ten directions hear their voice and immediately respond with praise.
Third, they have all already abandoned all dharmas that lack merit;
fourth, they have all already attained the true dharmas of merit, whereby they immediately obtain the seal of the Hero of the World.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva maintains the dhāraṇī of all affairs and understands them all without exception.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Having fully mastered supernormal powers, He flies through the air and purifies the multitudes of defilements."
That wisdom is exceedingly vast and expansive, universally equal to space.
All Tathāgatas see and hear their voice;
their responses are entirely complete, and that voice lacks nothing.
All non-virtuous deeds have been completely abandoned;
having attained auspiciousness through joyful love, one establishes the root of all virtues.
For those who abide thus, they are able to illuminate this Dharma.
"Within these merits, there shall be none who harm themselves.

When the Buddha spoke these verses on the four matters, twelve thousand people conceived the aspiration for unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment, and five thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena.
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and its great radiance shone everywhere.

In the first fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Devaputra Susīma*, from the second line at the end of the nineteenth folio—between the passage "when a person gives rise to the thought of supreme, true, and correct enlightenment" and the passage "five thousand bodhisattvas"—the Danben (Bezeklik) edition contains thirty-eight lines, beginning with "turning the wheel of the Dharma, sweet teaching, compassionate teaching," and continuing through "even unto the practice of nirvāṇa, never again falling into saṃsāra.

In the Songben (Song) edition, this corresponds to about fifty lines of scripture. Upon examining the textual characteristics, these passages are redundant from beginning to end and are all unsatisfactory; they are simply the concluding text of the eighth chapter, the "Vibhaṅga-parivarta," found in the third fascicle of the Song edition and the lower fascicle of the Dan edition.
The Dan edition repeats "re-established here," which is an error; therefore, it has not been added.
Please examine its meaning in detail.

Then, the Son of Heaven Suḥṛd spoke to the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
“The Tathāgata has bestowed upon me this Dharma chapter of thirty-two items and phrases; I only pray that you will explain it further in detail so that I may understand it.
How does a bodhisattva maintain unforgetting faith in the intention of this Mahāyāna?”
Mañjuśrī replied, “It is because the mind itself attains internal conviction and does not follow the teachings of others.
The devaputra asked again:
"What is it that makes a bodhisattva’s actions firm and steadfast?
He replied,
"Because they subdue and abandon all desires."
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva obtain the most excellent merit?
He replied:
"Because they realize the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) without wavering.
The Devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain unimpeded conduct?"
He replied,
"Because I am not deluded by the sense bases (*āyatana*).
The devaputra asked again:
"What is meant by 'a bodhisattva departing from the dust of darkness'?
He replied:
"Because one knows that all dharma-realms are fundamentally pure."
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva enter into assemblies with courageous eloquence and remain free from all fear?
He replied:
"Because when one seeks all dharmas, their form cannot be apprehended.
The Son of Heaven asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva obtain the meaning of what they have heard, and how do they rely upon it to maintain protection?"
He replied,
"Because one knows all dharmas through silence.
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain proficiency in the analysis of the Dharma?
He replied:
"Because they already know how to abide within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)."
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain compliance with the teaching?
He replied:
"Because they do not follow after various sounds.
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain accordance with the teachings of the Dharma?"
Mañjuśrī replied,
"Because they have attained all liberations.
The devaputra asked again:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva being one who has attained faultlessness?
He replied:
“Because the mind does not waver regarding all phenomena.”
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva subdue the hosts of Māra?
He replied:
"Because one awakens to emptiness through love and desire while seeking the Way.
The Devaputra asked again:
"In what way is the wisdom of a bodhisattva unattainable?"
Mañjuśrī replied,
"Because he has attained all the Buddha-dharmas and fully upholds them.
The devaputra asked again:
"How is it that a bodhisattva is not defiled by worldly dharmas?
He replied:
"Because they act in accordance with worldly conventions, they cannot be defiled."
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain all profound practices?
He replied:
"Because they do not fear the dharma of emptiness.
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva know the faculty of skillful means?"
He replied:
"Because one perceives the root of all sensory faculties within the six sense organs.
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain the gates of liberation?
He replied,
"Because they preach the teaching of liberation for all gates."
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain extraordinary skillful means?
He replied:
"Because one seeks nirvana within saṃsāra and perceives it there, and because one perceives the path of saṃsāra within nirvana.
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain the skillful means of causal conditions?"
He replied:
"By abiding in the incalculable, one perceives all phenomena.
The devaputra asked again:
"What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding the precepts? He replied,
"It is because one views all dharmas as having no point of attachment."
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain skillful means (upāyakauśalya)?
He replied:
"Because they act in accordance with worldly affairs, neither remaining detached from them nor becoming attached to them.
The Celestial Son asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain auspicious vows?"
He replied,
"Because I have attained the knowledge of the Path.
The devaputra asked again:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the power of patience? He replied:
"Because from the very beginning until the attainment of nirvāṇa, they fully know all dharmas."
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain the further shore?
He replied:
"Because they fully know all diverse phenomena.
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva bring benefit to all?"
He replied,
"Because they fully know the inexhaustible dharma-realm.
The devaputra asked again:
“How does a bodhisattva become beloved by the multitude?
He replied,
“By viewing all buddha-fields as being devoid of form.”
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva obtain the praise of the multitude?
He replied:
"Because one does not claim with regard to any phenomena that 'this is mine' or 'this is not mine.
The celestial son asked again:
"How is it that the virtues of a bodhisattva are inexhaustible?"
He replied:
"Because they know all phenomena to be equal to space.
The devaputra asked again:
“How does a bodhisattva make firm their fundamental vow?
He replied:
“Because they do not cause any destruction within the dharma-realm.”
The devaputra asked again,
"How does a bodhisattva become noble and honored?
He replied:
"Because, being without mind, they fully know all minds.
The Devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva become a teacher?"
He replied,
"Because in the dharma of non-conceptualization there is nothing to be relinquished.
The devaputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva come to understand all matters?
He replied:
"By knowing that all phenomena (dharmas) have no basis and no refuge, and because they neither come nor go."
"Therefore, O Son of Heaven!
A bodhisattva attains clear understanding of all matters.
When Mañjuśrī spoke these words, eighty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
How delightful it is that the meaning of the Dharma has been explained and analyzed in such a manner!"
3. Chapter on the Purity of the Dharma (2). In the *Sūtra of the Son of Heaven Susīma*, Chapter Three: "The Purity of the Dharma. Thereupon, the son of heaven Susīma again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Benevolent One!"
"Is the Dharma I inquire about pure and refined?
He replied,

"Regarding all that exists in the world, to desire them yet never be satisfied, and then to completely renounce them with the mind and examine the profundity of the Dharma— this is what constitutes the purity and refinement of the Dharma."
"Is what I have reported to you in response to your question truly a pure and virtuous Dharma?
As for the Dharma, O Son of Heaven,
it is neither pure nor virtuous."
Why is this so? Because it is devoid of form and appearance.
This, O Son of Heaven, is the nature of dharmas!
It cannot be seen. Why is this?
That which is perceived by the eye does not reach the ultimate subtlety, because it functions through attachment to existence.
Is it not so, O Son of Heaven!
That there is likewise no creator? Why is this?
Because it is without arising,
O Devaputra, there is no path to the Dharma.
Why is this? Because there is no "mine" and no self.
This is the nature of phenomena, O Son of Heaven!
All are entirely equal. Why is this?
Because they are like empty space.
"O Son of Heaven! The Dharma cannot be equaled. Why is this so?"
Because it is without companion.
It is the nature of things, O Son of Heaven!
To abide eternally, neither coming nor going; without speech or discourse; without disparagement or praise, being free from disparagement and praise.
It is without artifice or ornament, for it is neither ugly nor coarse.
Thus it is with the Dharma, O Son of Heaven!
It is without perforation or leakage, and without patching or seams.
Why is this? Because it transcends the conduct of Māra.
Is this not so, O Devaputra?
There is no growth and no nourishment. Why is this?
Because it is free from arising and ceasing.
Is it not so, O Son of Heaven?
The Dharma has no location and no abode. Why is this?
Because one delights in the dharma-realm.
O Devaputra, as for the Dharma,
it is fearless.
Why is this so? Because they are not deluded.
This, O Son of Heaven, is the nature of the Dharma!
There is nothing to be cherished. Why is this?
Because it is free from arrogance.
Is it not so, O Son of Heaven?
One must not be arrogant. Why is this?
Because one practices quiescence,
O Son of Heaven! Is it not so that the Dharma consists in practicing quiescence?
Why is this? Because it is free from all conceptual thoughts.
Such, O Devaputra, is the nature of dharmas!
There is no conceptualization. Why is this?
Because it subdues all heterodox paths.
Is it not so, O Son of Heaven?
There are no nests or dens. Why is this?
Because... [the text continues].
Because it is free from lust, anger,
and delusion, O Devaputra, the Dharma is empty.
Why is this so? Because it has been pure from the very beginning.
This, O Devaputra, is the nature of dharmas!
There is no ideation. Why is this?
Because there are no sounds or names.
Is it not so, O Son of Heaven?
There is no wish. Why is this?
Because consciousness is not constructed.
O Devaputra, as for dharmas,
they are without construction.
Why is this so? Because there are no boundaries.
This is the nature of phenomena, O Son of Heaven!
There is nothing to rely upon. Why is this?
Because it is non-dual.
"Is it not so, O Son of Heaven!
Do not waver. Why is this?"
Because it abides firmly.
O Heavenly Son, is it not the case that dharmas are without self?
Why is this? Because they are non-extinguished.
This is the nature of phenomena, O Son of Heaven!
There is no person. Why is this?
Because from the very beginning, there has been nothing produced.
Is it not so, O Son of Heaven?
That all things are impermanent. Why is this?
Because there is nothing that arises.
O Devaputra, as for dharmas,
they do not arise.
Why is this? Because one practices that which is unarisen.
Is this not so, O Son of Heaven?
There is nothing that arises. Why is this?
Because there is no perception of a vessel of suffering.
Is it not so, O Son of Heaven?
There is no conceptualization. Why is this?
Because it is free from all marks.
Thus, O Devaputra,
this is the meaning of the purity and excellence of the Dharma.
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! Since phenomena are non-existent and have no objective referent, why do you, O Venerable One, discourse upon the pure and virtuous Dharma?”
He replied, “Excellent, excellent!
Just as you have spoken, it is indeed no different.”
That which is "nothingness" (anupādāna) is precisely the pure and virtuous discourse on the Dharma. Why is this so?
Because there is no action performed by body, speech, or mind; this is the purity and virtue of the Dharma.
Why is this so? O Son of Heaven!
It is because the Dharma has no nest or lair.
Regarding those who dwell in nests and caves, if their body and mind are at variance, it constitutes an untimely mental gift.
The Son of Heaven asked again:
“How can one know that it is an untimely mind?”
He replied: "Devaputra!
When one possesses a body that is bound by the signs of the six decays (ṣadāyatana) yet reckons it to be permanent, one knows this to be an untimely mind."
To know the Dharma while seeking fame and becoming attached to sounds and echoes, thereby following a deviant path—this is to know the untimely mind.
To know the Dharma and the Sangha while receiving the realization of the fruits of the Path—this is to know the untimely mind.
To know that giving while being rooted in the false characteristics of desire is to know an untimely mind;
to know the precepts yet remain detached from tranquility is to know an untimely mind.
Having exhausted the three evil realms and attained rebirth as a human, if one sets one's mind solely upon celestial blessings, one knows this to be an untimely state of mind.
If one’s mind is undisciplined yet desires to practice giving, one knows this to be an untimely state of mind.
If the mind lacks tranquility, one knows it is an untimely state of mind.
If the mind relies on external support while seeking to practice patience, one knows it is an untimely state of mind.
If one seeks to exert diligence without purifying the mind, one knows it is an untimely state of mind.
To be prone to excessive thoughts and easily forgetful, with meditation and contemplation lacking stability, is to know the mind that is untimely.
To be self-important and arrogant, neglecting wisdom, is to know the mind that is untimely.
If one dwells in the notion of "mine" while wishing to practice loving-kindness, one knows this to be an untimely state of mind.
If one is intent on hesitation while wishing to practice compassion, one knows this to be an untimely state of mind.
If one who has fallen into the four [wrong] practices desires to practice joy, one knows this is a mind of untimely intent.
If one who dwells in the body of existence desires to practice protection, one knows this is a mind of untimely intent.
If one has no sensations of bodily pain or itching yet desires to contemplate the Dharma and does not cease doing so, one knows this is a mind of the improper time.
If one knows that the various arisings and ceasings [of phenomena] should not be severed, one knows this is a mind of the improper time.
If the body and mind are mutually dependent [on external objects] rather than relying on the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*), one knows this is an untimely state of mind.
If the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are dependent upon the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), one knows this is an untimely state of mind.
By the power of what is seen, relying upon the five powers, one knows the mind that is untimely.
By knowing that the seven factors lack the awakening-factors (bodhyaṅga), one knows the mind that is untimely.
If one contemplates sensual desire and greed as being incompatible with the Eightfold Right Path, one knows this is an untimely mind.
If one harbors doubt regarding the knowledge of suffering, one knows this is an untimely mind.
To have doubt regarding cultivation is to know it as a mind out of its proper time.
To have doubt regarding cessation is to know it as a mind out of its proper time.
To carry worldly attachments while seeking to enter the Way is to know it as a mind out of its proper time.
"In this way, O Devaputra!
Because one grasps at and becomes attached to a pure mind, one then knows it as a mind that is untimely.
The Devaputra asked again:
"How can one know the mind of that time?
He replied, "O Devaputra!"
"When the mind is equal to space, then one knows the mind of that moment.
He asked again:
"In what way is the mind like space?"
He replied:
"As space is without mind, so too is the mind.
Such a mind is equal to space."
He asked again:
"Who will possess faith that is equal to space?
He replied:
“Son of Heaven!
Those who calculate in terms of a self, a person, or an individual do not have faith.
The Son of Heaven asked again:
"If one calculates 'me,' 'self,' or 'person,' what is it that constitutes them?
He replied:
"The mind is equal to empty space, yet one desires to augment it and exceed beyond it."
He asked again:
"In what way does it increase and surpass them?
He replied:
“Those who reckon things as permanent wish to transcend them; those who reckon things as impermanent also wish to transcend them.
Those who reckon things as suffering wish to transcend them; those who reckon things as pleasure also wish to transcend them.
Those who reckon things as sorrowful wish to transcend them; those who reckon things as sorrowless also wish to transcend them.”
Those who conceive of a self-body also desire to transcend it; those who conceive of no self-body also desire to transcend it;
even emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness they desire to transcend.
Illusions, dreams, the moon reflected in water, shadows, and echoes—all dharmas are like these metaphors.
If one wishes to go even beyond such states as these, then by abiding in accordance with the Dharma, one may achieve further increase;
yet lust, anger, and delusion continue to rely upon one another, and one still desires to go even beyond them.
To disparage this cycle of birth and death and praise the matter of nirvāṇa, while further desiring to transcend it—
thus it is, O Devaputra!
This is what is meant by one who calculates in terms of "I," "self," "person," and "individual."
He asked again:
"How does one attain freedom from anger and not become stubborn?
He replied:
"Emerging from birth and death, they abide in *nirvāṇa*.
Returning to the world, they extinguish all cravings and practice purity.
They do not remain eternally in cessation, nor do they arise from arising; they are not terrified by forms or sounds."
Thus, for one whose practice is cessation, there is liberation; for one whose practice is liberation, such matters are already transcended.
No phenomena can extol their achievement or surpass their virtue; this is what it means to be without anger and without resentment.

When this Dharma was being taught, thirty-two thousand devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye; five thousand bhikṣus attained liberation of mind; and twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the power of patience.
Chapter Four: The Śrāvakas (2). The Sūtra of the Son of Heaven Suṣīma, Chapter Four: The Śrāvakas. Thereupon, the Son of Heaven Suṣīma addressed the great disciples:
"Venerable sirs, regarding that which you doubt, you may question Mañjuśrī."
The Elder Mahākāśyapa stepped forward and asked Mañjuśrī,
“How does a bodhisattva practice the eight meditative concentrations (aṣṭavimokṣadhyāna)?
He replied:

“The bodhisattva’s meditations on the eight liberations, the meditation of fundamental non-arising and non-constructing, the meditation of non-anger, and the meditation of equanimity—these are the bodhisattva’s meditations.
He asked again:
“Why do you speak thus?”
He replied: "O Kāśyapa!
The body is fundamentally non-existent; it is because there is no creator established within the three realms that craving and desire arise."

Having already realized detachment from desire, one therefore knows that the body is fundamentally non-existent; one creates nothing within the three realms, has no conceptualizations regarding desire, and having known emptiness, establishes meditative concentration.
In this way, Kāśyapa, it is said:

the eight stages of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the concentration of original non-existence and non-constructing, the concentration of non-anger, and the concentration of equanimity— these are the concentrations of a bodhisattva.
Thereupon Kāśyapa remained silent and spoke no word.
The Venerable Śāriputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain unimpeded wisdom?"
He replied:
"The Bodhisattva harbors no resentment toward obstacles, feels no restrictive attachment toward hindrances, and perceives all cravings with full knowledge without abandoning them."
"Why is this? Because he nurtures and protects all beings, the Bodhisattva attains unimpeded wisdom.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana asked again:
“How does a bodhisattva attain the bases of supernormal power?
He replied: “O Maudgalyāyana!...”

The Bodhisattva, regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), has no reception; he liberates all beings and brings them to their end, yet he does not have any reception within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Why is this so?
Because they protect and sustain all beings, the bodhisattva attains great supernormal power (mahā-ṛddhi).
The Venerable Subhūti asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva come to know the mental conduct of others?"
He replied: "O Subhūti!

A bodhisattva thoroughly understands all other diverse dharmas; his mind never tires of the work of the Path, and he constantly delights in samādhi without ever being satisfied. He manifests whatever actions are required; for this reason, a bodhisattva is able to know the practice of others' dharmas."
The worthy Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva extensively gather various meanings to explain the Dharma of clear wisdom?
He replied:

"O Pūrṇa! The Bodhisattva fully reveals all faculties, preaching their virtues according to what each delights in—namely, the principles of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self—causing each to attain their proper place."
Throughout countless births and deaths across hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he upholds the meaning of this Dharma and teaches it everywhere without exhaustion.
Such is his wisdom; therefore, the Bodhisattva extensively gathers various meanings to elucidate the Dharma of clear intelligence.
The worthy Revata asked again:
"In what way does a bodhisattva delight in dhyāna as is his constant practice?
He replied:

“O Vīrā! When a bodhisattva practices samādhi and fully knows all dharmas, they give rise to great compassion for those with distracted minds, causing them to initiate immeasurable practices; since there is no delight in non-meditation, the bodhisattva attains dhyāna.”
The venerable Upāli asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva come to uphold the treasury of the Dharma?
He replied:

“O Upāli! A bodhisattva fully knows the profound treasury of all dharmas; having been in *nirvāṇa* from the very beginning and being free from craving and desire, they have already accorded with the Dharma-treasury to instruct all beings, acting to demonstrate craving and desire so that they may awaken to and know them.”
"By causing the aspiration for the Way to arise amidst sensual desires, the Bodhisattva thus attains the profound treasury of the Dharma.
The Venerable Aniruddha asked again:
"How does a Bodhisattva attain the divine eye of penetrating vision?"
He replied: "O Ānanda!

When a bodhisattva has fully perceived all forms throughout the ten directions, he manifests the cultivation of form within all phenomena; yet he manifests non-attachment toward them all, causing those who follow his traces to attain liberation. This is the bodhisattva’s divine eye of penetrating vision."
The worthy Bakula asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain the tranquility and concentration of the sense faculties?
He replied:

“A bodhisattva regards all realms as the realm of the Buddha, and within the realm of the Buddha, they regard all realms as non-existent; therefore, the bodhisattva attains the tranquility and concentration of the faculties.”
The worthy Aṅgulimāla asked again:
"In what way does a bodhisattva obtain sharp faculties?
He replied:
"A Bodhisattva regards all those who commit the heinous crimes as being like the Path; therefore, the Bodhisattva attains the sharpness of the faculties.
The worthy Mahākātyāyana asked again:
"How does a Bodhisattva attain the skillful means of discerning and knowing the various sūtras?"
He replied:
“A bodhisattva attains the four kinds of inexhaustible equanimity. What are these four?”
First is the meaning, second is the Dharma, third is the sequence, and fourth is the response.
These are the four.

With a single verse, one may extensively analyze and expound the teaching for all beings throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas; yet this teaching does not approach the conditioned, is not subject to defilement, and being already pure, it cannot be repudiated.
Yet this teaching does not waver or shift within the realm of all phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), yet it acts as the recipient for all sensations.
For this reason, the bodhisattva attains the analytical knowledge of the skillful means of the various sūtras.
The worthy Mahākauṣṭhila asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain the four matters of meaning, dharma, sequence, and response?
He replied:
"A bodhisattva, having attained this regarding the quiescent dharma, instructs through equality of meaning;
abiding in the dharma, they instruct through equality of the dharma;
and being ever joyful and without resentment in what they do, they instruct through equal sequence."
Yet the resonance cannot be maintained; it is through repaying the instruction that one does so.
Therefore, the bodhisattva attains the meaning, the Dharma, the sequence, and the repayment.
The Venerable Rāhula asked again:
“How does a bodhisattva attain purity of precepts?
He replied: “O Rāhula!
"By means of the samādhi of pure precepts, the bodhisattva relinquishes both the observance and the violation of precepts to nurture all beings; therefore, the bodhisattva attains pure precepts.
The Venerable Ānanda asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain extensive learning?"
He replied:

"A bodhisattva desires to hear all that is spoken by the Buddhas; having heard it, they accept its meaning, and having heard it, they retain it all. Having heard it, they then teach it to others. This is how a bodhisattva attains extensive learning."
Thereupon, the great disciples rejoiced and remained silent.
At that time, the Devaputra Susīma addressed the great disciples, saying:
"Regarding the Dharma taught by Mañjuśrī just now, do you, venerable sirs, truly possess such qualities?"
The great disciples said,
"We ourselves are not yet able to fully comprehend even a single dharma, let alone as many dharmas as those.
The devaputra said:
“O Benevolent One!
Although there are various kinds of bodies, each distinct from the others, their underlying principle is one.
The great disciple replied:
"Just as the water in a cow's footprint, such is the knowledge of all other disciples.
As for the water that collects where the hub of a chariot wheel has pressed into the earth, we of our kind are like that."

For example, the waters of the great ocean are vast and expansive, without limit or boundary, and so deep that its bottom is difficult to reach; among śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattva is the most honored.
The devaputra praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
What you have spoken is most sincere and free from arrogance."
Mañjuśrī said: "It is so, O Devaputra!
What the disciples have spoken is not out of arrogance; their praise of the bodhisattvas is indeed accurate and true."
The devaputra asked Mañjuśrī,
“Virtuous One!
Why do you speak thus?”
He replied: "It is so, O Devaputra!
Do śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas rely upon arrogance?"
"To be free from arrogance?
A bodhisattva’s arrogance surpasses that of those others; to gather and assemble the Buddha-dharma—this is for the bodhisattva to practice with courageous vigor.
The devaputra asked again:
“Does the Bodhisattva act with arrogance because he wishes others to praise him?
He replied,
“It is because he wishes to guide all beings.”
"It is so, O Devaputra!
The Devaputra asked again:
"In what way is it so?"
He replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
For this reason, the Bodhisattva employs skillful means to praise the Buddha Vehicle and disparage the Disciple Vehicle."
Within the great assembly, he manifests his own bodily conduct and religious activities.
Why is this? It is because he desires to cause all beings to resolve upon the Great Way (bodhicitta), and does not wish for people to give rise to the mind of the Lesser Vehicle.
Why is this? Because it scorches and destroys the seeds of the Buddha;
therefore, I teach all people to distance themselves from it entirely.
Why is this? It is because one does not wish to cause people to become attached to or delight in it.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
"It is because he wishes to cause bodhisattvas to set forth in the Mahāyāna and to eliminate the vehicle of the disciples.
The devaputra asked again:
"Is this not an error?"
He replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
One praises the mani-jewel, lapis lazuli, and crystal for being exceedingly pure and unstained by anything."
"Is there anything further than this?
The Son of Heaven replied,
"What has been spoken is beyond reproach."
He replied: "It is so, O Devaputra!
A bodhisattva praises the Mahāyāna!"
To disparage the vehicle of the disciples is neither an increase nor a decrease [in the Dharma].
O Son of Heaven!
It is like a son of a great householder who praises the merits of a Wheel-Turning Sage King while reviling the poor beggars within the kingdom; would there be anything improper in this?
The devaputra said:
“There is nothing that cannot be done, Mañjuśrī!”
"Is it as you have described?
He replied, "It is so, O Devaputra!"
"When a Bodhisattva praises the Mahāyāna and disparages the Śrāvaka-yāna, there is no harm done.
At that time, the Buddha praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
What has been thus spoken is most excellent.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!
To praise the Mahāyāna while disparaging the Śrāvaka-yāna is to disparage all vehicles. Why is this so?
Because the Mahāyāna gives birth to all vehicles.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Devaputra Susīma, Scroll Two.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Devaputra Susīma, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Five: Fearlessness (3). In the fifth chapter, "Fearlessness," the Devaputra Susīma again asked Mañjuśrī:
"From what does a bodhisattva generate the aspiration for enlightenment?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra,
a bodhisattva gives rise to the thought of enlightenment from all desires."
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī, why do you speak these words?"
Mañjuśrī replied: “Devaputra!
It is when a bodhisattva engages in sexual desire within the midst of craving that they then achieve the Way.”
"If one does not follow after desire and craving, by what cause and condition, then, can a bodhisattva give rise to the aspiration for all paths?
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
“From what source does the mind establish itself upon the Path?
Mañjuśrī replied, “Devaputra!”
One establishes the aspiration for the Way within all the Buddha-dharmas.
Why is this so? O Devaputra!
"The aspiration for the Way fundamentally arises from the teachings of all Buddhas.
The Devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!..."
“From where do all the Buddha-dharmas arise?
Mañjuśrī replied, “O Devaputra!”
All Buddha-dharmas are fundamentally non-existent and have no arising.
Why is this? O Devaputra!
"Just as space is fundamentally non-existent, all Buddha-dharmas arise from the fundamental nature of space.
The Devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"How many are all the Buddha-dharmas?
Can they be known by counting? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Son of Heaven!
As all phenomena (dharmas) are equal, so too are the Buddha-dharmas. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata has attained perfect awakening to all phenomena as they truly are.
Therefore, O Devaputra,
just as all phenomena are equal, so too are the enumerations of the Buddha-dharmas equal.
The devaputra asked again: "How so, Mañjuśrī?"
“Are lust, anger, and delusion truly the Buddha-dharma?
Mañjuśrī replied, “They are.”
"O Son of Heaven!
Lust, anger, and delusion are themselves the Buddha-dharma. Why is this so? "
"Because they are taught and instructed by the teachings of the Way, their sensual desires are without conceptualization.
The Son of Heaven asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"Will it not be that all shall attain Buddhahood?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
All shall surely attain Buddhahood; you shall certainly become Buddhas.
Do not harbor any doubt. Why is this?
"Son of Heaven!
This is because all shall attain the right awakening of a Tathāgata.
The son of heaven asked again:
“Mañjuśrī, how is it that all attain Buddhahood? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Son of Heaven!
It is for the sake of entering into tranquility and for the sake of entering into emptiness.
The Son of Heaven asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! How are quiescence and emptiness to be realized? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! If emptiness cannot be apprehended, how can awakening be attained?
This is because emptiness has no companion, and is neither strong nor weak.”
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! Does the Tathāgata attain the Way by understanding emptiness?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "So it is, O Devaputra."
As you have said!
Emptiness is itself the Path.
The Buddha taught that understanding emptiness constitutes entering the Path.
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! Regarding the practice of emptiness, how should one practice it?"
Mañjuśrī replied, "Devaputra!
To practice without desire for form is itself the practice of emptiness."

Regarding the activities of the desire realm, they do not engage in the activity of sentient beings, nor the activity of fragrance; nor do they engage in the activity of form, nor the activity of the formless; nor do they engage in the activity of the body, nor the activity of the mind.
"Why is this? Because non-practice is itself empty.
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! Does the Tathāgata not practice this practice of fundamental emptiness? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
The emptiness of the Tathāgata is likewise empty; that which is non-existent therein is also thus for me.
As there is no movement, so is the movement of the Tathāgata.”
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! Since there is nothing that exists, what should one practice?”
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!

Just as there is nothing that exists, one should practice non-existence; one does not practice anything else, for even in other things there is non-existence, and such practice itself is also non-existent."
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! If there is nothing at all, what do you bring with you?”
Mañjuśrī replied: "O Devaputra!
