To be amidst sensual desire yet remain free from desire is what is called 'non-existence' (akiṃcana)."
Within sensual desire, one practices non-existence; when greed, anger, ignorance, and desire are neither desired nor undesired, it is therefore called "non-existence.
Not practicing within desire is called "non-existence."
"To dwell in the practice of emptiness by means of this very self is called 'non-existence'; to practice this non-existence is itself non-existence.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"What is it that one practices such that there is nothing? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"To practice tranquility is to have nothing; this is emptiness, this is seclusion, this is non-arising, and there is nothing that originates. To practice tranquility is to have nothing.
The Devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What kind of activity is called 'cultivation'?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
To be without destruction or decay is called cultivation.
To clearly understand all that exists without being defiled is called cultivation.
To be immeasurable and equal to space is called cultivation.
"To be free from arrogance and always to illuminate all things—this is called 'cultivation.
To be neither too much nor too little—this is called 'cultivation.
The Devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! What is it that is not practiced with understanding? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
One who does not know the practice of dharmas is said to be unacquainted with practice.
The Son of Heaven asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! What is meant by ‘one who is awakened regarding the formative forces (saṃskāra)’? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
One who knows the cultivation of dharmas is one who understands cultivation.
The Son of Heaven asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! What are the characteristics of not placing blind trust in the mind? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
The practice of being free from all obstructions is its characteristic.
The Son of Heaven asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! If a bodhisattva does not place blind faith in their own mind, how do they repay the grace of the faithful offerings bestowed upon them? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra!
One whose mind does not place false trust is said to have seen all phenomena with the eye of wisdom, and thus does not follow the teachings of others in matters of faith.”
One whose mind does not falsely believe does not further requite the grace of faithful offerings. Why is this?
Because from the very beginning, all things have been utterly pure.
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! Why is it that a bodhisattva who has shaved off his beard and hair refuses to enter the assembly and does not follow its instructions? What is this called?”
"What should one do in such a case? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
Because the Bodhisattva Who Has Removed His Hair and Beard refuses to enter the assembly and does not follow others, he is called the most steadfast in the world.
Why is this so, O Devaputra?
That which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in its actions is called the Saṅgha.
Because the Bodhisattva does not abide in the unconditioned nor cease within the unconditioned, he is therefore called the most profound of all in the world.
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! If a bodhisattva were to dwell correctly in the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), what fault would there be?"
Mañjuśrī replied: “Devaputra!

If a bodhisattva dwells in the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and fails to benefit all beings, they will fall into the practice of the disciples (śrāvaka) for the sake of extinction (nirvāṇa); this is their fault.”
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! The unconditioned is the ground of the Eightfold Path; the conditioned is the ground of ordinary people.”
“Because a bodhisattva dwells on the level of an ordinary person, is he not the most compassionate in the world?
Mañjuśrī replied, “Devaputra!”

"No. Why is this? Because a bodhisattva dwells neither in the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nor in the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); for this reason, they are called the most profound in the world."

Why is this? Because when Bodhisattvas initiate their practice, they ultimately abide within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); they do not dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nor do they construct the unconditioned. For this reason, they act as a source of sustenance for the world.
Abiding in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), one fully knows what is appropriate and inappropriate;
abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one knows the locus of all wisdom.
Having known what is appropriate and inappropriate regarding the conditioned, one dwells therein; having known the wisdom of the unconditioned, one does not abide therein.
“Devaputra!
It is like a valiant and powerful man who, having drawn his bow and fixed an arrow, shoots it upward into the sky; the arrow neither remains in the sky nor falls back down.
Mañjuśrī said to the devaputra:
"Is this difficult?
The Son of Heaven replied,
"It is extremely difficult, it is extremely difficult."
Mañjuśrī said: “The deeds performed by a bodhisattva are even more difficult than this. Why is that? Because—”
"Without abandoning the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), one attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); therefore, while abiding in the unconditioned, one nurtures and protects all within the conditioned.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"Does the fear of a bodhisattva arise from the conditioned,
or does it arise from the unconditioned? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra!
A bodhisattva’s fear arises from two causes and conditions: it arises from both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Why is this so?
"One fears craving within the conditioned, and one fears non-craving within the unconditioned.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"If one has no desire even for existence, why would one fear anything more? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"To not draw near to the three realms is itself a fear.
Not drawing near to the three realms constitutes falling into the stage of a disciple.
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! How does a bodhisattva attain fearlessness? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Son of Heaven!

A bodhisattva constantly practices the wisdom of wisdom within the conditioned; by means of the wisdom of skillful means, they do not fall into the unconditioned. This is how a bodhisattva attains fearlessness.”

Furthermore, O Devaputra, because of all things, the bodhisattva does not abandon the conditioned; because of the Buddha-dharma, he does not fall into the unconditioned. This is how the bodhisattva attains fearlessness.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!
All the causes and conditions of a bodhisattva’s meritorious giving are proximate to the conditioned;
all the causes and conditions of their Buddha-wisdom do not fall into the unconditioned.
This is how a bodhisattva attains fearlessness.

Furthermore, O Devaputra, when a bodhisattva abides in the conditioned, he has established meditative concentration; when he abides in skillful wisdom, he returns from that concentration. This is how a bodhisattva attains fearlessness.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!

When a bodhisattva abides in the mind of the Way, they give rise to meritorious qualities; when they abide in great compassion, they extensively protect all beings. This is what it means for a bodhisattva to attain fearlessness.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!

When a bodhisattva dwells in solitude and recognizes the deeds of Māra, and having skillfully established himself in expedient means, subdues the activities of Māra, this is called a bodhisattva attaining fearlessness.
Furthermore, O Devaputra,

when a bodhisattva dwells in universal great loving-kindness while preaching the Dharma, and dwells in great compassion while practicing various forms of giving, this is called a bodhisattva attaining fearlessness.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!

A bodhisattva dwells within birth and death while planting the roots of nirvāṇa, and dwells within nirvāṇa while planting the roots of birth and death; this is what it means for a bodhisattva to attain fearlessness.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!

A bodhisattva is "born" within non-arising; he is "born" within the conditioned. Regarding the phenomena currently perceived, he does not praise the five aggregates or the six sense-bases; he perceives them all as detached and non-arisen, tranquil and utterly stilled.

Not burning when not ignited, yet within that state of being ignited and burning, there is nothing produced; they fully embrace all cravings without being defiled by those cravings. Both those who study and those who do not study are already subdued;

they do not regard the liberation of disciples as something extraordinary. Entering human form, they do not abandon the Dharma-body; they manifest their conduct within the realm of Māra, yet remain unreleased from the Dharma-realm. Through wisdom they enter the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and through skillful means (*upāya*) they return from the unconditioned. They manifest themselves in many ways, enduring all that is acceptable and unacceptable with equanimity.

"The Buddha manifests that which one should always contemplate with joy to behold; the Dharma manifests that which is free from doubt. This, O Son of Heaven, is how a bodhisattva attains fearlessness. **Chapter Six:
Abiding in the Path (3)** *The Sūtra of the Son of Heaven Suṣīma*, Chapter Six: Abiding in the Path. At that time, the Son of Heaven Suṣīma again asked Mañjuśrī:
"How does a bodhisattva abide in the Path?"
Mañjuśrī replied, “O Devaputra!
A bodhisattva teaches the dharma for extinguishing desire, yet does not seek its realization within that extinction of desire.”
He teaches the Dharma for extinguishing lust, anger, delusion, and all cravings, yet he does not seek realization therein.
Therefore, O Devaputra,
the bodhisattva abides in the Way.

Furthermore, O Devaputra, when a bodhisattva speaks of emptiness, he does not take emptiness as a basis for realization; when he speaks of signlessness, he does not take signlessness as a basis for realization; when he speaks of wishlessness, he does not take wishlessness as a basis for realization; when he speaks of non-union, he does not take non-union as a basis for realization; when he speaks of non-arising, he does not take non-arising as a basis for realization; when he speaks of the unoriginated, he does not take the unoriginated as a basis for realization; when he speaks of the absence of limits, he does not take the absence of limits as a basis for realization; when he speaks of detachment from craving, he does not take detachment from craving as a basis for realization; when he speaks of detachment from activity, he does not take detachment from activity as a basis for realization; when he speaks of the cessation of phenomena, he does not take the cessation of phenomena as a basis for realization. This is what it means for a bodhisattva to abide in the Way.

Furthermore, O Devaputra! A bodhisattva fulfills the dāna-pāramitā by having nothing to bestow; fulfills the śīla-pāramitā by not upholding precepts; fulfills the kṣānti-pāramitā by possessing anger; fulfills the vīrya-pāramitā by means of indolence; fulfills the dhyāna-pāramitā by delighting in distraction and forgetfulness; and fulfills the prajñā-pāramitā by being intent upon folly.
"Therefore, O Son of Heaven,
a bodhisattva is able to abide in the Way.
The Son of Heaven asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! For what reason do you speak thus? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! There are four things that cannot be given as gifts.
What are these four?
First, not abandoning anything;
second, not abandoning the Dharma;
third, not abandoning the aspiration for enlightenment.
Fourth, not abandoning all merits.
These are the four dharmas that are not abandoned, by which one fulfills the dānapāramitā.
O Devaputra!
One observes the precepts because the mind has not yet been tamed;
once the mind is tamed, one relinquishes the precepts.

Having relinquished the precepts, one emerges from darkness; having emerged from darkness, one has attained illumination. Having relinquished illumination, one attains equanimity; having relinquished equanimity, one attains wisdom; having relinquished wisdom, one attains liberation and the manifestation of wisdom.
"Son of Heaven, you should know that it is by thus relinquishing the precepts that one fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
Son of Heaven!

If this bodhisattva, while disparaging the vehicle of the disciples (śrāvaka-yāna) and praising the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna), has already praised the Great Vehicle as the ultimate Great Vehicle, he thereby fulfills the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā)."
"O Son of Heaven!
If this bodhisattva does not deceive through body, speech, or mind, then they act without indolence; such a dharma constitutes the perfection of *vīrya* (diligence)."
"O Son of Heaven!
Suppose this bodhisattva, even in a dream, does not mentally cling to the two extremes. Why is that? "
Because they do not delight in the vehicle of the disciples or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
Having no delight in the vehicles of the disciples or pratyekabuddhas, they proceed toward the Great Vehicle.
Having reached the Great Vehicle, they fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā.
"O Son of Heaven!
All dharmas are delusion; they are like grass, trees, walls, tiles, and stones—such is the nature of folly.

Because one has long practiced seeing the meaning of feeble and inferior delusion, all things are rooted in the dharma of delusion. By means of wisdom and insight, one is fully prepared for the Path; thus, one possesses the Prajñāpāramitā."
"O Son of Heaven!
What has been done is as it should be; this is how a bodhisattva abides in the Way.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!"
The Bodhisattva does not abandon the traces of birth and death, nor does he seek the traces of Nirvana; he neither interrupts these traces nor constructs them, and he abides nowhere.
For those who enter onto wrong paths, he establishes the Right Path; this is what it means for a Bodhisattva to abide in the Path.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!
A bodhisattva seeks all persons and searches for all dharmas, yet neither attains any person nor attains any dharma.
Why is this? Because they do not abandon the bodhisattva path.
What they say is sincere and all is effective; this is what it means for a bodhisattva to abide in the path.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!

A bodhisattva knows that the path of the śrāvaka is without expectation, and knows that the path of the pratyekabuddha is likewise without expectation; he knows the bodhisattva path, fully perfecting its faculties and fulfilling all merits, and only thereafter does he follow it—this is called the bodhisattva’s abiding in the path.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!

A bodhisattva engages in all that is performed within birth and death, yet does not receive the fruits of those actions. The nature of such associations cannot defile him; he dedicates all merits toward the vow for the Path, seeing no path other than non-retrogression.
Why is this? Because they are fully perfected.
This is what it means for a bodhisattva to abide in the Way.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
When a bodhisattva seeks the Way within the Way, yet does not enter parinirvāṇa, this is called a bodhisattva abiding in the Way.
The Devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! How can one seek the Path while already within the Path?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“Son of Heaven!
It is because of birth and death that it is called the Way.
The Bodhisattva seeks the Way because he desires to liberate all beings.”
"All things are non-existent; there is nothing to be sought, nor is there anything to be delivered.
The celestial son asked again: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"Is the path entered by all the worlds the practice of a bodhisattva?
Mañjuśrī replied, "It is so, O Devaputra!"
"It is exactly as you have said: that which is entered by all the world is the bodhisattva practice.
Why is this? It is thus, O Devaputra!"
Moving through the world, they are not defiled by worldly dharmas.
Following after desire, they manifest as desireless, yet they do not fall into the state of desirelessness;
within birth and death, they manifest the knowledge that all dharmas are neither born nor arisen.
Being without hope for glory, one does not seek realization within that state of being without hope for glory;
one maintains [the view of] the five aggregates and six sense-decadencies while remaining detached from the five aggregates and six sense-decadencies as "not mine.
Seeing and knowing those who maintain the five aggregates and six sense-decadencies, one preaches the Dharma to them all.
The five aggregates and six sense-bases are empty and non-existent, and they cannot be seen.
Having realized their non-existence, one then attains the application of mindfulness through dhyāna.
When samādhi and samāpatti are unified as one, one attains the stilling of the mind, and the mind becomes firmly established.
Having attained firm abiding, one is then able to enter universally into the minds of all people.
If the mind does not cease, it will take pleasure in the hosts of Māra.

The Bodhisattva is not defiled by the deeds of Māra and does not abandon the Buddha-realm; while acting in accordance with whatever occurs within the realm of Māra, they do not waver from their station within the Dharma-realm; and while in the realm of human beings, they bestow protection upon sentient beings. This is called the Bodhisattva’s diligence that accords with all worldly conduct.
Chapter Seven: The Conduct of Bodhisattvas (3). At that time, the Devaputra Susīma again asked Mañjuśrī:
"What is meant by the bodhisattva’s practice of diligent application?"
“Please explain this for us; we wish to hear it.
Mañjuśrī replied, “O Son of Heaven!”
To have no activity is the most pure conduct worthy of veneration.
Having already attained abiding in this bodhisattva practice, one lacks nothing among all things that exist; having performed what was to be done in seclusion, one’s purpose is fulfilled.
To have one's intention fixed upon the Way is the practice of non-forgetfulness; for the mind and intention to be equanimous is the practice of giving;

for the mind and intention to be disciplined is the practice of precepts; for the mind and intention to be tranquil is the practice of patience; for the intention not to be weary is the practice of diligence;
for body and mind to be still and silent is the practice of meditative reflection; [to dwell] within the practice of the dharma-realm is...
To be detached from all that exists is the practice of wisdom; not to act for the sake of the unattainable is the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
that nothing at all exists is the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); that desire is not the self and that which is done is already empty is the practice of sympathetic joy (*muditā*);

to be vast and free of thought is the practice of equanimity (*upekṣā*); and to have no aspiration for the realms of gods or humans is the practice of tranquil concentration (*samādhi*). Thus one fully understands.

The practice of the knowledge of suffering consists in the realization that all phenomena are suffering; the practice of the knowledge of dependent origination consists in regarding the aggregates as like an illusion;

the practice of the knowledge of cessation consists in the realization that the absence of wisdom and its like are to be extinguished; the practice of the knowledge of the path consists in the analytical classification for the sake of cessation; the practice of the knowledge of causes consists in the lack of delight in aggregation;

the practice of the knowledge of conditions consists in the thorough understanding that the aggregates are indeed conditioned; and the practice of the convergence of both consists in the definitive resolution of meaning and discipline.

The meaning of having no location and remaining silent without speech is practice based on the Dharma; the indestructibility of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is practice based on cessation (*nirodha*);
the non-existence of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is practice based on retribution; being like sound and like an echo is practice based on the aforementioned meaning;
manifesting the possession of marks and signs is practice based on the wisdom of the body; and the adornment of the body and faculties is based on the sūtras.

Wandering in emptiness and repenting of one's own transgressions is the practice of precepts; knowing the minds of others is the practice of the divine eye; the purification of transgressions is the practice of the divine ear;
the extreme purity of the precepts is the practice of knowing the minds of others; the completion of all transgressions is the practice of past lives;
calculating the three miserable realms and so forth is the practice of the divine feet; and the attainment of mastery over the mind is steadfastness.
Forceful action that is indestructible is essential practice; being unmoved and unshaken is the practice of peaceful creation;
being unshivering and unstartled is the practice of equanimity; constant mindfulness of having no refuge is the practice of space;
observing and fully knowing is the practice of illusion; the appearance of adornment is the practice of a dream; and the appearance of boundaries is the practice of a mirage.

The practice of non-accumulation is the practice of the shadow; the practice of non-greed is the practice of the echo; the practice of definitively discerning the characteristics of the Vinaya is the practice of the mirage;
the practice of the characteristic of vagueness is the practice of emptiness; the practice of the characteristic of the divisions of the body is the practice of non-conception;

the practice of the characteristic of the divisions of the mind is the practice of wishlessness; the practice of the characteristic of the divisions of the three realms is the practice of non-encounter.

Meeting and dividing into parts is the practice of subduing Māra; that mind, intellect, and consciousness do not exist and do not manifest is the adamantine practice of never severing the Three Jewels;
that all things are augmented is the characteristic of this practice.
"Such a mind, O Son of Heaven, is the practice of the bodhisattva’s path.
Chapter Eight: Differentiation (3) At that time, the Devaputra Susīma again questioned Mañjuśrī:
“Does a bodhisattva who abides in the Path have a practice that has already surpassed those of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
Mañjuśrī replied, “It is so, O Devaputra!”
It is exactly as you have said.
The practice of a bodhisattva truly surpasses that of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?

There is neither faith nor realization; neither upholding the Dharma, nor the eightfold path; neither the srotāpanna, nor the sakṛdāgāmin, nor the anāgāmin, nor the arhat; neither the pratyekabuddha, nor the tathāgata, nor the samyaksaṃbuddha, nor the śrāvaka.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
If one does not know this and does not reckon that "this is a bodhisattva," then one is a bodhisattva.

One does not reckon it as a worldly dharma, nor as a dharma of lust, nor as a dharma of anger, nor as a dharma of delusion, nor as a dharma of birth and death, nor as a dharma of nirvāṇa; if one does not know this and does not reckon that "this is a bodhisattva," then one is a bodhisattva.
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī, why is it so?"
"For what reason does a bodhisattva attain faith and realization up to the dharma of nirvāṇa?
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!"
The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands and has faith in all dharmas as being entirely detached; they have no attachment to desires and do not believe in other paths. Why is this?
Because they believe in the path of the six pāramitās.
Having attained faith, one then upholds it; those who are bound and attached, one delivers and liberates.
One constantly seeks the wisdom of the unconditioned; one fears neither birth-and-death nor does one feel dread toward nirvāṇa. For this reason, the bodhisattva attains the essential core of faith.
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva attain the essential dharmas for upholding?"
Mañjuśrī replied: “Devaputra!

The Bodhisattva upholds all the teachings and instructions spoken by all Buddhas; he finds no pleasure in worldly flavors, taking the Dharma as his food and drink. Established in the meaning of the Dharma, he does not dwell in sensual desire. Thus, he attains the power of the Dharma rather than worldly power; he attains the meaning of the Dharma rather than valuing worldly meanings; he attains the dignity of the Dharma rather than worldly dignity; he attains reliance upon the Dharma rather than relying on persons. He proclaims the Middle Way of the True Dharma and does not speak what is non-Dharma. Abiding in the place of the Dharma, he does not abide in non-Dharma. Through the Dharma, he penetrates all things with clear vision, free from obstruction or hindrance, thoroughly knowing all phenomena. Having attained *dhāraṇī*, he possesses true and unforgetting awareness. With the seven precious jewels, he is fully endowed with treasures; relying upon all phenomena, he then dwells in the state of sovereign mastery over the Dharma.
"Therefore, O Son of Heaven,
a bodhisattva attains the essential dharma.
The Son of Heaven asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! How does a bodhisattva attain these eight matters? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! The Bodhisattva emerges from the eight heterodoxies and, through the practice of pure meritorious deeds, follows the eightfold right path; having fulfilled his vows, he enters the Way.
All people in the world who dwell in the eight difficult conditions likewise abide therein.”

In order to attain the eight perceptions of a man in a place free from hardship, he constantly aspires to the mind of enlightenment without relinquishing it, and attains the eight *dhyānas* of exertion; for these reasons, the bodhisattva attains these eight matters.
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva enter the stage of srotāpanna?”
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!
A bodhisattva regards all people as being like those who have fallen into the ocean and are carried away by the downward current."

There are those of great strength who travel upstream against the current, severing the flow of birth and death without destroying their fundamental practice, thereby attaining the equal severance of the paths of the three evil realms.

They cause all beings to attain a place of peace and security, remain far removed from hesitation, dwell truthfully within the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, transcend the tracks of ordinary people, delight in establishing the tracks of the Buddha-dharma, and, having understood the limit of birth and death, turn toward the gate of Nirvana.

Possessing the foremost depth among all beings in the world, he constantly establishes people in the resolve for nirvāṇa, leading them toward the Way so they may reach the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Clearly manifesting instruction on transcending birth and death, he demonstrates the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and extols it, sharing in the equal joy of the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
"For this reason, the Bodhisattva attains entry into the stage of Srotāpanna.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"How does a bodhisattva attain entry into the stage of a sakṛdāgāmin?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
The Bodhisattva, knowing all future and yet-to-occur phenomena, enters into the cycle of birth and death to protect all beings and preach the Dharma for them, leading them to the unconditioned state.

One does not perceive any dharma that reaches the unconditioned; nor does one perceive its coming, nor its abiding. Although it manifests as coming, it is free from craving and desire; when it departs, its task is complete.

Coming, they do not contravene the fundamental essentials; coming, they do not follow the teachings of Māra; coming, they arrive at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); coming, they uphold the teachings of all Buddhas and manifest them; relying upon all dharmas, they come to protect all beings, causing them to cross over the abyss of birth and death; having attained the path of firm and powerful supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they cannot be destroyed by anyone.
"For this reason, the Bodhisattva attains entry into the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin.
The Devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"How does a bodhisattva attain entry into the stage of an Anāgāmin?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
The Bodhisattva does not turn back from anything he perceives; he does not follow the aggregates (*skandha*) or the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), nor does he fall into any perversions (*viparyāsa*).
In this state, he does not turn back; he neither comes nor goes.
In this state, he does not turn back; he does not follow teachings that are contrary to the Dharma, and he is without fear, without lustful desire, without hatred, and without delusion.

No longer returning, his deeds are ever victorious; he is fully perfected in the Buddha-dharma. His merits in going and coming are equal and without distinction; all that was to be done has been completed, and there is no further assembly.

Having already received the prediction of enlightenment, one does not give rise to what ought to be created; that which is not under one's own control is transcended through wisdom, and the wise do not depend upon others for service.
"For this reason, a bodhisattva attains entry into the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin).
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"How does a bodhisattva attain entry into arhatship?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
The Bodhisattva completely renounces all possessions, subdues greed and desire, and preaches the Dharma for the sake of all beings.
Those who harbor anger he subdues, instructing them with the Dharma to eliminate their wicked dispositions; those who are deluded he subdues, transforming them through the Dharma.

Having realized that all phenomena are like an empty village, they do not abandon anything, but exert themselves in the teachings of the Buddhas; their minds take no pleasure in the world, for they see that all unions and gatherings are impermanent, and thus they are always preeminent among those who make offerings.

Just as a lotus flower is unsullied by mud and water, being without self, without grasping, and possessing nothing, one should maintain meditative equipoise upon all phenomena and constantly keep them in mind; through wisdom, one discerns emptiness and establishes one's resolve according to what others delight in.

The aspirations of his past lives have all been fulfilled; his mind remains steadfast and does not follow the teachings of others; he accepts neither the praise nor the blame of any speech; having attained resolution with joy, he uses that resolution to deliver all beings across.
"Therefore, a bodhisattva attains entry into arhatship.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"How does a bodhisattva enter the path of the śrāvaka?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
To preach all those dharmas that a bodhisattva has not heard is the way of a śrāvaka.

To have no faith in the Śrāvakayāna, yet to cause those who have not heard it to hear it—that which is neither produced nor arisen within the dharma-realm regarding all attached phenomena—is the way of a bodhisattva.
Regarding those who rely on various causes and conditions, they have already heard repeatedly that there is no self and no person.
This teaching of emptiness is not limited to the Buddha-dharma; the dharmas they practice are like the void, which gives rise to the essentials of all phenomena.

Hearing [the Dharma], they are constantly diligent and free from all obstructions; though they hear the Dharma from others, they do not merely accept and practice it as taught by them; being thus established in dhyāna, they do not follow the instructions of others, and they fully understand and know all sounds of the past, future, and present.

Having severed what was to be done and being incapable of exhaustion, he considers himself fully accomplished; furthermore, having attained the inexhaustible analogies and meanings of the Dharma, he thoroughly knows the mental conduct of all people.
They manifest through wisdom to guide and benefit others, preaching the Dharma according to their inclinations so that they may reach their destination without arrogance,
while constantly fulfilling their original vows.
"For this reason, a bodhisattva is able to enter the stage of the śrāvaka.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"How does a bodhisattva enter the stage of a pratyekabuddha?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"

When a bodhisattva gains access to the conditions and understands that all phenomena are without self, without person, without life-span, without vital principle, and without a master who adorns them—being deceptive and unreal, belonging to nothing—the characteristics of their causal conditions are likewise so.

To perceive all causes and conditions clearly, to take the Path as one's food and drink, and not to abandon the rules of discipline—these are the companions of the perfections; and the realization of all paths is the companion of the Dharma.
To be free from arrogance regarding the four debts of gratitude is the companion of supernormal powers.
To know the law of causes and conditions without falling into attachment, and not to believe in other karmic paths, is to attain the way of equal enlightenment.

One perceives and knows the locus of faith without harboring divergent thoughts, and does not follow the ruinous path of the merits of the Hīnayāna; rather, one establishes the Mahāyāna by practicing all dharmas through causes and conditions.
"For this reason, a bodhisattva is able to enter the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"How does a bodhisattva attain Buddhahood? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Son of Heaven!"

The Bodhisattva fully awakens to the knowledge that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and quiescent; he awakens to the knowledge that all things are fundamentally non-existent; and he awakens to the knowledge of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Regarding the evil realms, among humans, and in the heavens, his mind is entirely detached from all worldly pleasures and comforts.
Why is this? Because they have fully understood all wisdom.
Through their own mental realization of wisdom, they know that all desires are empty and that their own bodies are likewise empty; by means of a single moment of mindfulness, they awaken to the Way.
Next, without turning toward anything else, he immediately manifests countless and manifold phenomena.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood.
The Devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! How does a bodhisattva attain the state of a Tathāgata? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
A bodhisattva comes by way of the Tathāgata’s path.
Suchness is the truth; there is not a single path that is forgotten.”

Suchness is that which establishes; Suchness is that which bestows; Suchness is morality; Suchness is patience; Suchness is diligence; Suchness is single-minded concentration; Suchness is wisdom; Suchness is skillful means; Suchness is insight; Suchness is neither human nor non-human. It manifests as a human being to practice the severing of birth and death, and among all conditioned phenomena, it emerges equally above them.

Those who deliver others from fear reach the further shore; yet those delivered have no "there," nor do they abide in "there," nor do they reach "here," nor do they abide in "here. Because they are fundamentally pure, they transcend both places.
Distant from darkness, one views light with equanimity; regarding darkness as neither darkness nor non-darkness, one transcends darkness.
The Tathāgata comes from emptiness, dispersing defilements and causing them to return to emptiness.
"Therefore, the Bodhisattva attains the state of a Tathāgata.
The Devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"How does a bodhisattva reach the place of *pulkaka* where birth and death are destroyed?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
The Bodhisattva destroys craving and desire, attaining liberation from the realm of birth and death within the three worlds.

While manifesting the state of non-existence within the state of existence, he causes all people to cast off their heavy burdens and subdue the hosts of Māra. He causes those who delight in and cling to various places to distance themselves from them, leading them to lay down their burdens and sever their ties to those locations.

He perceives everywhere the various states where good and evil arise; having departed from those places, he delights in renouncing lust. With a supple mind, he stabilizes his body and mind through meditative concentration, remaining fixed in precepts and wisdom. He fully beholds all evil states and remains detached from them without clinging. He enters into all bodies and understands every condition, guiding and benefiting beings at the very points of birth and death through the bestowal of merit. He extensively establishes bridges and constantly delights in making offerings, fulfilling and covering the three realms without ever becoming weary or negligent, and thus becomes one who is venerated and looked up to by the people of the triple world.
"For this reason, the Bodhisattva attains the *nipakaprabha* [stage].
The Devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"How does a bodhisattva attain the equal awakening of the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
The Bodhisattva’s mind is impartial toward the five heinous crimes as it is toward the Right Path; therefore, there is no awakening that is not equal.
It is equal toward what is seen and the four inversions, and equal toward the aggregates and all obscurations that veil the Path; thus, there is no awakening that is not equal.
Lust, anger, and delusion, as well as all desires, are equal to the Path; therefore, there is nothing that is not equally awakened to.

The dharmas of ordinary people, the dharmas of practice and non-practice, the dharmas of *pratyekabuddhas*, and the dharmas of *bodhisattvas* are all equal to the Path; therefore, there is nothing that is not equally awakened to.
"Therefore, a bodhisattva attains the state of Samyak-saṃbuddha.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
“How does a bodhisattva attain the state of the World-Honored One,
the Vairocana? Mañjuśrī replied,
“O Devaputra!”
The Bodhisattva instructs worldly people so that they may attain merit and that anger does not arise.
Those who hear his teachings all uphold them; when he teaches what is not the Dharma, it serves as the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
It is the sweet teaching, the compassionate teaching, the teaching of the trichiliocosm, and the teaching for all World-Honored Ones.

It is that which receives the self-refuge of all; it is that which acts as the lamp-light for all; it is the most brilliant light among all lights; it is that which brings about the tranquility of all; and it causes all people to be without conceptual thought, extinguished rather than blazing.
He resolves all doubts for all people, and all difficulties arising from doubt are completely severed for them.
He increases the merit of all people, and is honored by the Wheel-Turning Kings, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, and Brahmā.
When slighted by the foolish, he feels no resentment; when praised by the wise, he feels no joy.
His mind is ever equanimous, like empty space; the World-Honored One is supreme, being equal toward all in the world.
"For this reason, the Bodhisattva attains the state of a Lokottara.
The Devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
“How does a bodhisattva enter the dharma of ordinary people known as *pāṣaṇḍa*?
Mañjuśrī replied, “O Devaputra!”
A bodhisattva performs all the actions of ordinary people, manifesting through skillful means the conduct of all common folk, yet knowing them to be without attachment.
For this reason, the bodhisattva is able to enter into the dharmas of ordinary people.
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva enter the *lekhādhāra* dharma of lust?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!

A bodhisattva is constantly sorrowful and weeps because he desires to attain the Buddha-dharma; he constantly longs for and delights in perfecting his body so that it becomes like the body of a Tathāgata; and he directs loving-kindness toward all beings without any anger."
"Therefore, the Bodhisattva is able to enter into the dharma of lust.
The Devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"How does a bodhisattva enter the dharma of *stīna-uddhata-dveṣa* (sloth,
agitation, and hatred)? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"

A bodhisattva perceives eighteen matters within a single matter; to them, the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are like enemies, and they do not encourage others to give rise to such activities.
While manifesting desire within the conditioned, his mind remains unattached to that desire.
Why is this? Because he desires to nourish all beings.
"Therefore, a bodhisattva is able to enter into the dharma of anger.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"How does a bodhisattva enter into the dharma of delusion,
the *mūḍhatā-lana*? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
The absence of any cognition or awareness is called delusion (*moha*).

Regarding the states of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) that are practiced through the cultivation of non-cognition—these one neither knows nor understands; they neither breathe in nor breathe out; they are neither produced nor destroyed.
"Therefore, a bodhisattva is able to enter into the dharma of ignorance.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"How does a bodhisattva attain entry into the *saṃsāra* of the *samantataraṇa*?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
The Bodhisattva remains unmoved within birth and death.

Why is this? Because they seek the path of the Buddha, they abide firmly and do not waver; thus, no Māras can find an opportunity against them. They attain non-attachment toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), being equal toward birth and death as they are toward the Buddha-dharma.
Not delighting in the Lesser Path, but viewing the Great Path with equanimity, neither moving nor turning—
thereby the Bodhisattva is able to enter the phenomena of birth and death.
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! How does a bodhisattva enter the dharma of nirvāṇadhātu and parinirvāṇa?"
Mañjuśrī replied, “Devaputra!

A bodhisattva conforms to various worldly customs and manifests the path of nirvāṇa; yet, knowing all phenomena as habitual tendencies, he extinguishes them. While practicing the conduct of nirvāṇa, he does not pass into parinirvāṇa; while practicing the conduct of nirvāṇa, he does not enter eternal extinction.”
Therefore, the Bodhisattva attains entry into the dharma of extinction.
This concludes the third fascicle of the *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Devaputra Susīma*.
Fascicle Four of the *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Devaputra Susīma*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Nine: Verses (4). Chapter Nine on Verses.
Suḥṛddevaputra again asked the youth Mañjuśrī:
“How does a bodhisattva attain mastery over skillful means and wisdom so as to enter [the world] and teach according to worldly conventions?
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke these verses in song for the devaputra:
“The mind has no attachment to desires, Always resolved to seek the unsurpassed path.”
The eye practiced by the mind sees all; for this reason, it is the mark of wisdom.
Causing all to resolve their minds [on enlightenment] and always causing them to aspire to this path, with a mind that never abandons the path—such is the mark of skillful means (*upāya*).
All persons are likewise non-existent; the wise understand this clearly.
Having completely purified all things as empty and quiescent, for this reason it is the characteristic of wisdom.
Gathering all people together, those who possess bodies and are subject to attachments, he brings them to maturity through the Way and its Virtue; such is the mark of his skillful means.
The body is fundamentally empty, and it is likewise so; in that which is fundamentally non-existent, nothing is seen.
By relying on the three fields as already pure, this is therefore the characteristic of wisdom.
Giving away all that exists—head, eyes, body, and precious treasures—to establish the aspirations of all beings: such is the mark of skillful means.
Delighting in the purity of silence, not being conceited on account of one's precepts,
with body, speech, and mind all entirely stilled— this is the mark of wisdom.
Having fully perfected the precepts oneself, one also exhorts and praises those who uphold them;
since the Buddhas are all accomplished through the precepts, such is the mark of skillful means.
Attaining patience through the absence of self, realizing that all things great are likewise empty,
and being without deficiency or leakage in body, speech, and mind— this is the mark of wisdom.
Neither expressed by body nor speech, the mind does not give rise to distraction therein;
all phenomena are quiescent and pure—such is the mark of skillful means.
Always enduring all people, even when they revile or strike with staffs, one protects them all out of compassion and does not abandon them; for this reason, it is a mark of wisdom.
Fully understanding and believing in all merit, Exhorting and encouraging all people,
Constantly examining and practicing the path of discipline— Such are the characteristics of skillful means.
Constantly practicing samādhi and completely extinguishing all craving and desire, one does not engage in habitual attachment;
for this reason, it is the characteristic of wisdom.
Having cast aside all meditations that he finds pleasing, he manifests his conduct within city walls;
because he desires to compassionately guide all beings, such is the mark of his skillful means (upāya).
Neither here nor there, but already correctly abiding in the middle;
that which cannot be seen is thereby relinquished—this is the characteristic of wisdom.
Always remaining unsatiated with emptiness—such a one is one who understands emptiness;
they then compassionately protect all people—such is the mark of skillful means.
One sees the Buddha through the dharma of signlessness;
viewing it as equal to empty space, one dwells nowhere within forms and appearances. For this reason, it is the characteristic of wisdom.
Having already made offerings to ten billion buddhas, he is the hero among all who offer;
having fully attained the marks and signs of a buddha, such is the mark of his skillful means.
The Dharma is pure and free from the dust of lust; it views all things with equality as if they were empty space.
Since this Dharma is without anything to be grasped, it is therefore characterized by wisdom.
Having already established oneself within the dharma-realm, one’s undertakings are eternally consummate;
remaining unshakable therein—such is the characteristic of skillful means.
No one at all can know it; its dharma and meaning are likewise so.
When one examines its fundamental source, it is empty; for this reason, it is the characteristic of wisdom.
Neither arising nor ceasing, they fully understand all phenomena;
neither departing nor coming from anywhere—such is the characteristic of skillful means.
Wherever one is born, there is constant peace and security;
having no desire for form within the five aggregates, one always protects all beings—this is the mark of wisdom.
Constantly practicing in secluded places, without establishing a self or dharmas,
always reverently cultivating dhyāna and samādhi— such is the mark of skillful means.
In villages, hamlets, and cities, he teaches with gentle and supple tones;
never wearying of the Dharma he proclaims—this is the mark of wisdom.
Free from fear regarding the three periods of time, Abiding in neither suffering nor pleasure,
Having disciplined the faculties of the body and attained tranquility— Such is the mark of skillful means.
With a mind of equanimity toward the great assembly, and likewise toward those with sorrowful thoughts, he manifests his body within them all; such is the mark of skillful means.
Having fully practiced unimpeded wisdom, they never dwell upon names;
like space, they are equal and beyond all speech—it is for this reason that it is the characteristic of wisdom.
Appearing within the bonds of desire, he teaches the Dharma to the people and constantly praises the Triple Gem; such are the characteristics of skillful means.
Regarding the qualities of the supernormal powers, his mind is always well-regulated in tranquil samādhi;
abiding in the middle without being high or low, this is the mark of wisdom.
Possessing the supernormal powers of flight and transformation, he immediately travels to billions of buddha-fields;
there he makes offerings to billions of Buddhas—such is the mark of skillful means.
Viewing the aggregates as like an illusion, one has no attachment to the forms of desire;
thus one extinguishes all hosts of Māras—this is the mark of wisdom.
They manifest among all māras, and having manifested, they depart;
therein they deliver all beings—such is the characteristic of skillful means (upāya).
Constantly drawing near to the gate of deliverance, one immediately attains emptiness and the absence of conceptual thought;
by bestowing what ought to be bestowed, this constitutes the characteristic of wisdom.
Free from anger and malice toward those who are hateful, a mass of wisdom untainted by folly,
in whom no further growth or sprouts of affliction arise— such is the mark of skillful means.
Having already accomplished what was to be done through faith, one constantly practices the various wisdoms;
having fully transcended all the pāramitās, this is therefore the characteristic of wisdom.
Though manifesting as desire and delusion, it is like a rebuke for those who lack the faculty of wisdom;
by means of this, one protects all beings—such is the mark of skillful means.
Attaining equanimity as if in nirvāṇa, one is able to extinguish the mass of aggregates;
having already subdued the three realms, this is therefore the mark of wisdom.
In this world of birth and death, all people are one's friends;
never being satiated in the merit one performs—such is the mark of skillful means.
Through the eightfold right path, one attains emptiness and stillness; this is the wisdom of the bodhisattva.
With wisdom and skillful means, by following this vehicle, one becomes a Hero of the World.
Practicing with both skillful means and wisdom, neither arising nor existing;
with wisdom and skillful means together, one attains sagacity without arrogance.
Wisdom and skillful means always follow one another and proceed together, like two oxen yoked to a single pole;
such is the unsurpassed field for awakening to the Dharma.
10. Chapter on the Categories of the Path (4). Chapter Ten: The Categories of the Path. The Devaputra Susīma again asked the youth Mañjuśrī:
"What is the nature of the path?"
Mañjuśrī replied, “Devaputra!
That which I dwell in is the category of the Path.”
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! What is the locus that constitutes the locus of the Path?"
Mañjuśrī replied, “Devaputra!
Quiescence is the locus of the path.”
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! What is the characteristic of the Path?"
Mañjuśrī replied: “Devaputra!
Space is the characteristic of the Way.”
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! Where does the Way abide so as to constitute the Way?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!
To abide in empty space is itself the Way."
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! By whom is the Path established?"
Mañjuśrī replied: “Devaputra!
The Path is established through all dharmas.”
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! What is the root of the Path?"
Mañjuśrī replied: “Devaputra!
Equanimity is the very root of the Way.”
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! By what is the Dharma sustained so as to constitute the Way?”
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!
To maintain the absence of self and the absence of a person—this is why it is called the Way."
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! What is it that is equal to the Way?”
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!
That which is unproduced and unarisen is equal to the Way."
The devaputra asked again: “Mañjuśrī!
To what place does the Way go?”
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!
The Path proceeds into the midst of all the mental activities of the hearts of all sentient beings."
"Why is this? Because there is nothing practiced and nothing reached.
The Devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! From what does the Path arise? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Son of Heaven!
Great compassion is that from which the Way is born.
The Son of Heaven asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! How is it that great compassion is born from this path? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! To transcend all things is great compassion; this is the source from which the Way arises.
The Devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī, from where should the Path be sought? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
The Way is sought from within all desires.
The Son of Heaven asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! How can sensual desire lead one out of the way? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
Purifying the eightfold right conduct is therefore the Path.
The Son of Heaven asked again:
“Mañjuśrī, how can the eightfold right path coexist with sensual desire? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! These eightfold paths coexist with sensual desire; will you then praise the purity of the path?
Lust, anger, and delusion are themselves the path; as one practices sensual desire, so too does one practice the path.”
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! Within this practice, what is it that one does so as to be in accord with the Way?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!
Within this practice, one neither attains desire, nor attains birth-and-death, nor attains nirvāṇa; for this reason, it is the Way."
"The practice of the Way attains union with the Way.
The Son of Heaven asked again: "Mañjuśrī!
"What is the practice of a bodhisattva? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"The sixty-two views, the four inversions, the five hindrances of the aggregates, and all those who possess no merit—these are the practices of a bodhisattva.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the meaning of this? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
The Bodhisattva, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), extensively follows wherever beings enter, desiring to rescue and deliver them all.
All that is sought is sought only within various views, craving, and the four inversions.
Why is this so? Because everything arises from within this.
When one seeks therein, nothing at all can be found; neither the seer nor the seen can be found, nor can craving be found, nor can the four inversions be found. It is neither "all" nor "not-all."
Why is this? Because it protects and liberates all beings.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
"One should understand it thus: the bodhisattva path is sought amidst desire.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
“Does a bodhisattva not seek the Way by means of the three gates of liberation?
Mañjuśrī replied, “Devaputra!”
One cannot attain the Way through emptiness, nor can one attain it through signlessness, nor can one attain it through wishlessness. Why is this so?
"Because within this there is no mind, consciousness, or thought, nor is there any movement.
Only when there is movement of mind, consciousness, and thought does one accomplish the Way.
The Celestial Son asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! What practice is it that is called the Way? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! Ignorance is equal to the Path, and the Path is equal to ignorance.
To practice with such equality is called ‘equality of the Path.’”

Regarding right view and wrong view; regarding right mindfulness and wrong mindfulness; regarding right speech and wrong speech; regarding right livelihood and wrong livelihood; regarding right action and wrong action; regarding right effort and wrong effort; regarding right intention and wrong intention; regarding right concentration and wrong concentration.
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī, how is it that right view and wrong view are equal?”
Mañjuśrī replied: "O Devaputra!
It is equal to empty space; it is equal to tranquility."
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! What is the distinction between emptiness and tranquility?"
Mañjuśrī replied: “Devaputra!
Are ‘equality with non-existence’ and ‘equality with empty space’ different from one another?”
The devaputra replied to Mañjuśrī, saying,
“Equality with non-existence and equality with empty space are truly without difference. Mañjuśrī said:
“In this way, O Devaputra,
emptiness, stillness, and equanimity are likewise without distinction.
The Devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! How can that which is said to be equal yet still possess distinctions such as praise and eulogy? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! If one gives rise to self-conceit because of conceptualizing causes and conditions, there will be differentiation, which leads to being praised and extolled.
However, if one does not give rise to self-conceit because of conceptualizing causes and conditions, and understands the characteristics of this meaning, then there is no differentiation.”
For example, O Son of Heaven!
The myriad rivers and four currents each have their own names, yet they all flow back to the sea and merge into a single flavor. Why is this so?
Because there is no difference.
Thus, O Devaputra, those who do not clearly understand the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) claim that there is difference; those who clearly understand the dharma-realm see that there is no difference.
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! Can the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) be seen or known?”
Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
The dharma-realm cannot be seen or known."
Why is this? Because it synthesizes and gathers all dharmas.

Within the dharma-realm they do not cognize one another; yet, within this dharma-realm, through equal mindfulness, they attain the wisdom of the three periods of time. This is the locus of the dharma-realm.
To cast off the mind of distraction, confusion, and hesitation is to know its proper place.
To never accept confused speech is to know its proper place.
It is just so, O Son of Heaven!
Within formlessness, one perceives all forms; yet these forms are also non-existent, equal to empty space.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
Within the dharma-realm, which is utterly pure and free from defilement, the Bodhisattva perceives all dharmas just as one sees the reflection of one’s own face in a clear mirror.
“In this way, all these phenomena and the dharma-realm are equally pure like space.
The devaputra asked again: “Mañjuśrī!
“How does a bodhisattva attain eloquence and wisdom?
Mañjuśrī replied, “O Devaputra!”

The Bodhisattva, through the wisdom of the empty body, has nothing to sever; yet within all that is perceived, he manifests his own body to preach the Dharma of impermanence to all people so that they may become detached from this body—this is the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the wisdom of eloquence.
"Knowing all that exists as empty, one finds that there is nothing whatsoever in anything.
The devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"How does a bodhisattva attain the discernment of all dharmas?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
"Knowing emptiness and stillness, one does not differentiate between having a body and being bodiless; therefore, the Bodhisattva is able to discern all phenomena.
The Devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"How does a bodhisattva become a guide?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
The Dharma of a bodhisattva neither abides nor does it not abide.
Therefore, O Devaputra,
a bodhisattva is able to become a guide.
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī, how does a bodhisattva come to know a single matter and thereby comprehend countless matters?”
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!
A bodhisattva remains unmoved within the state of non-conceptualization; therefore, the bodhisattva knows one thing and fully comprehends countless things."
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! Can a bodhisattva indeed manifest entry into the three categories?"
"What are these three? They are:
being equal to the essential path, entering what is non-essential, and entering the deviant path.
Mañjuśrī replied:

“Devaputra! A bodhisattva enters the essential path regarding the Buddha-dharma; he enters the non-essential path regarding the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and he enters the path of perversion regarding the deliverance of all beings.”
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī, does a bodhisattva ever abide in seclusion or abide in bustle?”
Mañjuśrī replied, "Devaputra!
A bodhisattva has leisurely tasks."
The devaputra asked again:
"Why is it exactly so? For what reason does one enter into agitation?
He replied:
"He dwells in manifestation by means of various forms of diligence, nurturing sentient beings so that they may attain leisure. Why is this?
Because he regards all beings."
"O Son of Heaven!
The liberation of the śrāvakas is for their own sake. Why is this so? Because..."
This is what constitutes attaining leisure;
yet the bodhisattva does not manifest within it.
Furthermore, there are those who are anxious and distressed who all come seeking the Way, and the bodhisattva goes there to manifest himself.
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! Have you now attained leisure?"
"And why are you afraid?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
"I am neither fearful, nor am I conversant.
The Son of Heaven asked again: "Mañjuśrī!
"Why is this so? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
I have not yet reached anywhere, nor have I attained anything;
I am not familiar with stillness, nor do I dwell in it for even a moment or a single instant, for I am bound by birth and death.
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! When you speak these words of the Dharma, is it for the purpose of subduing the realm of Māra?”
Mañjuśrī replied: “It is indeed so,
O Devaputra!”
As you have said, noble one, this discourse on the Dharma is for the purpose of subduing the realm of Māra. Why is this so?
O Devaputra!

Such Dharma-teachings do not recognize the five aggregates, nor do they involve the renunciation of sensual desire, nor the arising of something within liberation, nor do they approach liberation or subdue heterodox paths.
Why is this so, O Devaputra?
Because all practices of heterodox paths are not contained therein; it is established as the firm Flower of the Dharma.
Why is this? Because there is no darkness, as all things are entirely luminous.
It is for the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and for the severing of all views.
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! Regarding these words of the Dharma you have spoken, how many people are there who can understand the world of the Dharma?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!
There is no world that is not darkness; this is precisely what is created by the world of dharmas."
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! That worldly people hear these words of the Dharma and attain liberation is truly something most difficult to encounter!"
Mañjuśrī replied: "O Devaputra!
Those who do not grow weary of the bonds of the world will believe in this Dharma; there is none among them who will not attain liberation."
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī, what is this that is called ‘weariness with the bonds of the world’?”
Mañjuśrī replied:

"To distance oneself from lust, anger, and delusion; to abandon craving and desire; and to seek liberation by awakening to the nature of suffering—this is what constitutes weariness with the fetters of the world."
The devaputra asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! Who, moreover, does not grow weary of the fetters of the world?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!
Because they are equal to lust, anger, and delusion; equal to craving and desire; and equal to liberation, they do not weary of the fetters of the world."
Thereupon, when the assembly heard these words of the Dharma, there was none who did not leap for joy; they all attained great gladness.
At that time, celestial flowers and sandalwood incense rained down.

The various devas likewise took up caskets filled with flowers and incense, scattering them over the Buddha and upon Mañjuśrī, while playing drums and stringed instruments and singing songs as they came to make offerings to the Buddha.

Hundreds of thousands of millions of devas praised the Buddha with gentle voices; moreover, they shook their robes in the air, leaping for joy with redoubled fervor, having fortunately been able to hear this Dharma.
At that time, all the people in the assembly, seeing this miraculous transformation, scattered flowers, incense, and robes over the World-Honored One and the youth Mañjuśrī, and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
Those who hear these words of the Dharma yet do not believe or understand them have failed to encounter the Buddha.

To claim that these words of the Dharma were not spoken by the Buddha is to be neither one who has shaved off their beard and hair nor one who upholds the great precepts; such a person neither recites nor takes joy in them, and is thus neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
Yet they do not follow this; such individuals lack the four virtues and possess no name.
Why is this? It is because of their fear and dread.

Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who possess faith upon hearing of these various supreme merits of the bodhisattvas, in order to reach the very bottom of birth and death and to sever all evil paths, shall receive and uphold this Dharma in the presence of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, and remain steadfastly established in it.

Upon hearing this Dharma, all shall thereby attain liberation. Those who receive, uphold, recite, and extensively explain its meaning to all others possess the purity and completeness of the precepts; they have encountered the Buddha; they have turned the wheel of the Dharma; they are śramaṇas; they are brahmins; they have shaved their hair and beards; they have received the full ordination; they have attained realization; and they have gained a true name.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised those in the assembly, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke to Maitreya:
"Uphold this Dharma; you should recite, chant, and read it, and expound it extensively for the sake of all beings.
While this sutra was being spoken, twelve nayutas of people were freed from dust and defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within them;
eight thousand bhikṣus attained liberation through the exhaustion of outflows.
Thirty thousand bodhisattvas resolved their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
fifty thousand bodhisattvas attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
“O Benevolent One, when you attain Buddhahood, all bodhisattvas and those present in the assembly shall likewise attain and uphold this Dharma.
Maitreya shall grant the prediction of enlightenment to all who hear, receive, and uphold this profound sutra.”
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Write down, uphold, recite, and receive this 'Chapter on Dharma Words,' and explain it extensively for the sake of all beings.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Receive and uphold it alone.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
“What is the name of this sutra?”
"How should it be practiced?
The Buddha said:

"This sutra is named 'The Questions of the Devaputra Susīma,' it is named 'The Response of the Youth Mañjuśrī,' it is named 'Severing All Doubts Regarding All Dharmas,' and it is named 'The Universal Entry into the Skillful Means and Wisdom of All Buddhas, the Discerning Illumination, the Instruction, the Retention, the Proper Retention, the Thorough Retention, and the Truthful Retention.'"
When these words of the Dharma were spoken, the immeasurable lands of the trichiliocosm quaked in six ways.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Devaputra Suviśuddhamati, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and others, as well as the venerable Ānanda and the great assembly, along with the devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and the people of the asura realm, were all filled with great joy; they prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
